findings.headline: Debt-to-revenue ratio increased to 2.5 in 2025-26, indicating higher leverage relative to income
findings.detail: The ratio of external debt to net service expenditure increased from 2.3 in 2024/25 to 2.5 in 2025/26 due to the £174m borrowing spike. The ratio is projected to improve to 2.3 in 2026/27 as the capital programme moderates and revenue continues to grow.
findings.matters: A debt-to-revenue ratio above 2.0 indicates material leverage; an upward trend signals increasing reliance on borrowed funds relative to the council's income-generating capacity
findings.figures: Debt to net service expenditure: 2.3 (2024/25), 2.5 (2025/26), declining to 2.3 (2026/27) and 2.2 (2028/29)
findings.quote: Debt to net service expenditure ratio  2.3 2.5 2.3 2.3 2.2

findings.headline: Interest costs forecast to rise 51% from 2024/25 to 2027/28, reaching £53.4m annually
findings.detail: Total interest payable grew from £35.3m in 2024/25 to £41.1m actual in 2025/26 and is forecast to reach £47.7m in 2026/27 and £53.4m in 2027/28. This substantial escalation reflects both the significantly larger debt stock and the impact of rising interest rates on refinancing.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs compress revenue flexibility and represent an increasing fixed claim on the council's budget relative to discretionary spending
findings.figures: Total interest payable: £35.3m (2024/25), £41.1m (2025/26 actual), £47.7m (2026/27 forecast), £53.4m (2027/28 forecast), £52.3m (2028/29 forecast)
findings.quote: Total Interest Payable & Expenses 35.3 41.1 47.7 53.4 52.3

findings.headline: External loans grew by £174.1m in 2025-26, with planned continued heavy borrowing through the capital programme
findings.detail: External loans increased from £900.0m to £1,074.1m in a single year. Forecasts show total external loans reaching £1,274.6m by 2028/29. This reflects capital expenditure of £209.9m in 2025/26 financed partly through borrowing (£101.1m), with projected borrowing of £176.1m for 2026/27 before declining.
findings.matters: The scale and trajectory of debt accumulation directly affects the council's debt service burden, financial flexibility, and credit risk from a lending perspective

findings.headline: 100% of cash investments exposed to bail-in risk, double the concentration of comparable London councils
findings.detail: Brent holds £43.8m in cash investments, all in money market funds with 100% bail-in exposure (risk of loss if the institution fails). This is substantially higher than comparable London authorities (80% bail-in exposure) and the wider local authority average (64%). The council acknowledges the risk but has not diversified into covered bonds or strategic pooled funds, keeping all liquid resources concentrated in bail-in-exposed instruments.
findings.matters: A failure of major financial institutions would directly threaten the council's access to working capital, forcing emergency borrowing at distressed rates and jeopardising payroll and supplier payments.
findings.figures: £43.8m cash investments at 100% bail-in exposure; comparable London authorities 80%; all local authorities average 64%
findings.quote: Whilst this highly liquid investment strategy provides maximum flexibility, it also means that 100% of Brent's investments remain subject to bail-in exposure, compared with 80% for similar London authorities and 64% across all Arlingclose local authority clients.

findings.headline: Working capital increased £70m through debtors, not cash, signalling potential collection or timing issues
findings.detail: The council's working capital rose from £89.6m to £159.2m, driven almost entirely by a £70m increase in debtors (receivables). However, the council explicitly states this increase did not translate into additional cash available for investment, with cash balances instead being drawn down to fund the capital programme. This anomaly suggests debtors are not converting to cash at expected rates.
findings.matters: If receivables are not converting to cash as expected, it indicates either collection difficulties or timing misalignment with expenditure. This affects cash flow management and may force additional borrowing to meet operational needs, further pressuring the balance sheet.
findings.figures: Working capital increased £69.6m; debtor increase approximately £70m; cash investments declined £3.5m
findings.quote: Although the Council's working capital increased during 2025/26, this was primarily driven by higher year-end debtor balances rather than additional cash resources. As a result, the increase in working capital did not translate into higher cash available for investment, with cash balances continuing to be utilised to support the capital programme.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing depleted by £115m in a single year while external borrowing rose £174m
findings.detail: The council's internal borrowing (use of own cash reserves to finance the capital programme) fell sharply from £453.8m to £338.2m. Simultaneously, external borrowing increased by £174m. Cash investments held for operations also declined from £47.3m to £43.8m. This represents simultaneous depletion of liquid resources and accumulation of external debt, narrowing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Declining reserves and rising dependence on external borrowing reduce the council's ability to absorb cash flow shocks, changes in capital programme timing, or market disruptions. It also increases refinancing risk if access to borrowing markets tightens.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing fell £115.6m (from £453.8m to £338.2m); external borrowing rose £174m; cash investments fell £3.5m
findings.quote: Cash balances continuing to be utilised to support the capital programme and debt repayments. Although the Council's working capital increased during 2025/26, this was primarily driven by higher year-end debtor balances rather than additional cash resources. As a result, the increase in working capital did not translate into higher cash available for investment.

findings.headline: New PWLB borrowing locked in at 5.7% for 10-year loans while existing portfolio averages 3.9%
findings.detail: The council raised £230m of new PWLB borrowing (EIP basis) in 2025/26, with 10-year PWLB rates at year-end 5.72% versus the council's existing portfolio average of 3.90%. As the council continues capital programme delivery, each new borrowing tranche locks in higher costs, raising the marginal cost of debt and increasing future interest payment burdens.
findings.matters: The gap between new borrowing costs (5.7%) and average portfolio costs (3.9%) means the council is substantially increasing its average debt costs. This matters for budgeting capital financing costs and servicing affordability of the capital programme.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB rate 5.72% (vs 5.38% at start of year); average debt rate 3.9%; £230m EIP borrowing raised
findings.quote: Whilst interest rates fell during the year, the rates available for new PWLB borrowing remained higher than the average rate payable across the Council's existing debt portfolio. Consequently, the addition of new borrowing increased the overall weighted average cost of debt, albeit only marginally.

findings.headline: Two LOBO loans refinanced at 6.4% and 6.2% following lender options, up from original rates of 4.1% and 5.2%
findings.detail: The council repaid £20m of LOBO debt when lenders exercised options in 2025/26, forcing refinancing into borrowing at costs 200+ basis points higher than original rates. Another £9.5m LOBO loan is due for a rate review in 2026/27 and faces the same refinancing risk. If exercised, the council will need to decide whether to repay with cash (worsening liquidity) or accept even higher borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Unexpected forced refinancing at elevated rates increases debt servicing costs and reduces budget flexibility at a time when the council is already taking on substantial new borrowing.
findings.figures: £10m repaid at 6.41%, £10m repaid at 6.24%; original rates 4.1% and 5.2%; £9.5m LOBO due for review 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council repaid two LOBO loans in 2025/26 after the lender exercised their option. As a result, the Council's borrowing requirement increased, with the additional financing being met through borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) during the year within our overall borrowing need.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Supported Exempt Accommodation costs spiked to £2.1m overspend in 2025-26; sector-wide regulation problem with uncontrollable liability
findings.detail: Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) was historically not a significant pressure. However, a £2.1m overspend occurred in 2025-26. The paper notes this is "a national challenge": providers are not bound by Local Housing Allowance (LHA) caps and can charge higher rents once claiming to provide support. Rent Officer determinations depend on provider claims, creating perverse incentives. The paper notes "need for clearer regulation regarding the criteria that providers must meet" and that clarity on minimal care requirements is needed.
findings.matters: This is an uncontrollable cost driver (provider-determined rents not subject to caps) that could escalate further. It signals both sector-wide regulation gaps and Brent's vulnerability to unscrupulous providers.
findings.figures: £2.1m overspend in 2025-26; being carefully monitored for 2026-27
findings.quote: Unlike other landlords, providers of supported exempt accommodation are not bound by Local Housing Allowance (LHA) caps and can charge higher rents once they demonstrate that support services are being provided... However, an overspend of £2.1m occurred in 2025/26 and this area of spend being carefully monitored.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme experiencing 5.5% slippage (£19.1m) with multiple schemes delayed due to planning and multi-stakeholder complexities
findings.detail: The capital programme is forecasting £326.6m expenditure against revised budget of £348m, a variance of £21.4m (£19.1m slippage, £2.3m underspend). Significant delays include: Gladstone Park Youth Centre (£3.0m, planning submission autumn 2026), Grand Union Canal (£3.2m design/planning delays), Staples Corner and Neasden (£2.2m combined), Affordable Housing schemes. Clock Cottages has exhausted its budget due to handover delays and requires additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital slippage can affect programme outcomes and indicates delivery challenges. Delays in affordable housing and regeneration could affect the council's ability to meet policy objectives.
findings.figures: £21.4m variance on £348m revised budget (6.1%); £19.1m net slippage; individual delays £1.1m to £3.2m; Clock Cottages needs additional borrowing
findings.quote: As at Quarter 1, the capital programme is forecasting expenditure of £32.6m against a revised budget of £348.0m for an overall variance of £21.4m. The £21.4m variance comprises net slippage of £19.1m and net underspend of £2.3m.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Building Control income structurally declined since October 2023 due to Building Safety Act regulatory change; unlikely to recover
findings.detail: Building Control income targets were set when income from major projects was significantly higher. Since October 2023, the Building Safety Act required Higher Risk Building applications to be charged on cost-recovery basis rather than as income-generating work. Combined with reduced development activity, this created "a sustained and structural reduction in income that is unlikely to reverse under the new regulatory regime". The current income target "requires review for current and future years to ensure continued alignment with CIPFA guidance". The service also faces workforce pressure from shortage of qualified surveyors.
findings.matters: This is a permanent structural loss of income that cannot be recovered. It will require permanent reductions, budget reallocation, or acceptance of lower service quality in a regulatory area.
findings.figures: Income reduction amount not quantified in extract; sector-wide surveyor shortage noted
findings.quote: Since the introduction of the Building Safety Act (BSA) in October 2023, Higher Risk Building applications must be made to the Building Safety Regulator and charged on a cost recovery basis. This change, alongside reduced major development activity, has resulted in a sustained and structural reduction in income that is unlikely to reverse under the new regulatory regime.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: HRA building safety remediation costs remain unquantified but comparable councils incurred ~£2.3m; council under regulatory scrutiny
findings.detail: The HRA received a C3 judgement from the building safety regulator. The council is delivering an improvement plan with ongoing regulator engagement. However, remediation and recovery costs are "still being quantified". The paper notes "comparable authorities reportedly incurring around £2.3m in similar circumstances". Additionally, there is a risk that grant funding for housing development could be restricted "while the Council operates under regulatory scrutiny, until full compliance is demonstrated".
findings.matters: The financial impact is material and unknown; regulatory weakness signals governance gaps. Restrictions on grant funding could affect housing delivery and regeneration ambitions.
findings.figures: Comparable authorities incurred ~£2.3m; Brent exposure unquantified; stock condition survey coverage now above 70% (target 100%)
findings.quote: remediation and recovery costs are still being quantified, with comparable authorities reportedly incurring around £2.3m in similar circumstances. There is also a risk to grant funding for housing development while the Council operates under regulatory scrutiny, until full compliance is demonstrated.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement shift toward complex cases poses a £3.5m latent overspend risk in otherwise breakeven directorate
findings.detail: The Service Reform and Strategy directorate is forecasting breakeven, but there is significant underlying risk in Adult Social Care. The budget was modelled on an assumed placement mix, but at Q1 the actual trend shows homecare demand has reduced while demand for supported living and residential care has increased with more complex needs. New packages are "around 14-16% more expensive than those ending". The paper explicitly quantifies this as "a potential risk of £3.5m overspend if this is not mitigated".
findings.matters: This represents demand-led cost escalation driven by ageing population and complexity increase. It's structural, not temporary, and similar patterns appear in other councils.
findings.figures: £3.5m potential overspend; new placements 14-16% more expensive than those ending; 6% increase in service users in 2025-26
findings.quote: In comparison to the 2026/27 modelling for Adults Placements that informed budget setting, at Q1 the trend indicates that homecare demand has been reduced but the demand for supported living and residential care have increased as with clients with more complex needs being placed, indicating a potential risk of £3.5m overspend if this is not mitigated.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council tax collection is behind target (19.2% vs 19.3% prior year at Q1) and business rates collection is weak (16.2% vs 17.8% prior year)
findings.detail: Council tax collection as at 31 May 2026 was 19.2%, 0.1% lower than the same period in 2025-26. The council is targeting 93.5% full-year collection but "improvements are required to collection across the remainder of this financial year in order to meet this target". Business rates (NNDR) collection is 16.2%, 1.6% lower than the same period in 2025-26, against a 95.5% target. The NNDR collection rate in 2025-26 was 94.1%, so the council is running materially behind pace.
findings.matters: Shortfalls in collection are funded from reserves or carried forward as deficits to next year. The council is currently tracking below target, which will constrain resources for the remainder of 2026-27 and create pressure into 2027-28.
findings.figures: Council tax: 19.2% collected (May 2026) vs 19.3% prior year; 93.5% full-year target vs 91.6% achieved in 2025-26. NNDR: 16.2% collected vs 17.8% prior year; 95.5% target vs 94.1% achieved in 2025-26
findings.quote: Based on the collection in the year to date, a similar or lower level of collection on the current year liabilities can be expected at the end of 2026/27, compared to previous years, meaning that improvements are required to collection across the remainder of this financial year in order to meet this target.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Economic environment has deteriorated since budget-setting; inflation and interest rates remain elevated, creating persistent cost pressure
findings.detail: Since February 2026, the economic environment has shifted. CPI inflation, expected to average 2.5%, instead reached just over 3% in March and eased only to 2.8% by April. The Bank of England now expects inflation to remain higher for the rest of 2026 than previously forecast. Interest rates remain at 3.75% versus the 3.25% expected in February. The paper explicitly states this creates "a risk of overspending in 2026/27" through higher pay awards and contract inflation, and increases borrowing costs for the capital programme.
findings.matters: Cost pressures are likely to persist throughout the year, increasing downside risk to the forecast and tightening the medium-term outlook. This will make the existing £9.5m and £18.2m overruns harder to manage.
findings.figures: CPI 2.8% (April 2026); Bank Rate 3.75%; expected to remain higher than 2.5% average budgeted
findings.quote: The Bank of England now expects inflation to remain higher for the rest of 2026 than previously forecast, compared with the February assumption of an average rate of 2.5%. Higher inflation increases the cost of delivering council services and creates a risk of overspending in 2026/27 compared with the budget agreed earlier in the year.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Housing Needs emergency: 1,428 households in emergency accommodation (up 9% since April 2025), driving a £9.5m General Fund overspend
findings.detail: The entire General Fund overspend is concentrated in Residents and Housing Services, specifically Housing Needs and Support. In April 2026 there were 1,428 households in nightly paid accommodation compared to 1,182 in April 2025. The service started the year already £3.7m overspent (despite £8m growth in the budget) due to the elevated baseline. Provider cost inflation has added a further £10 per night per placement above budget, potentially worth £3.9m in additional pressure. This reflects 8,795 homelessness applications in 2025-26 (169 per week, 21% increase year-on-year).
findings.matters: This is unfunded demand-driven overspend that's structural (homelessness at record levels) not cyclical, consuming the council's entire financial headroom. Rising applications indicate the problem will persist and likely worsen.
findings.figures: 1,428 households (April 2026) vs 1,182 (April 2025); £326/week average cost per person; £10/night cost inflation above budget; 8,795 homelessness applications (21% increase year-on-year); already £3.7m overspent at year start despite £8m growth
findings.quote: In April 2026, there were 1,428 households in nightly paid accommodation, compared with 1,182 households in April 2025. This represents an overall increase of 9% since December 2025, when 1,312 households were in accommodation, with approximately half of the annual increase occurring between Q3 and Q4.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Developer contributions (Section 106 / Community Infrastructure Levy) fund £151.7m of the £915.8m six-year capital programme (16.6%), creating vulnerability to development slowdown.
findings.detail: The capital financing table shows CIL and S106 contributions of £63.8m (2026/27) and averaging £30-31m per year thereafter, totalling £151.7m over the plan period. If development activity or new housing consents drop, this revenue stream shrinks, forcing the council to either cut capital or increase borrowing further.
findings.matters: Developer contributions are volatile and depend on market conditions outside council control. A housing slowdown could force unplanned borrowing at a time when interest rates may be unfavourable.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Interest payable rising 16% to £47.7m in 2026/27, reflecting refinancing of maturing debt at higher interest rates plus a £75.8m surge in new borrowing.
findings.detail: Interest payable jumps from £41.1m (2025/26) to £47.7m (2026/27). The borrowing requirement itself grew sharply: new borrowing in 2026/27 is £176.9m vs £101.1m in 2025/26, a 75% increase. Combined with refinancing existing debt at higher rates in a rising-rate environment, this drives the interest cost escalation.
findings.matters: If interest rates stay elevated or rise further, financing costs will accelerate. The council's affordability currently improves only because revenue is forecast to grow strongly; if that growth slips, interest cost becomes a constraint.
findings.figures: Interest payable £41.1m → £47.7m. New borrowing requirement: £101.1m (2025/26) → £176.9m (2026/27).
findings.quote: Total Interest Payable & Expenses 41.1 47.7

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Brent is funding a new £32m capital loan to i4B Holdings (its housing subsidiary) entirely from borrowing in 2026/27, on top of existing £179m subsidiary debt.
findings.detail: The council's loans to i4B Holdings rise from £179.2m to £211.2m in 2026/27, with this document explicitly noting a new £32m capital loan included from that year. Section (l) confirms all service investments (£326.4m total) are funded entirely by borrowing. This subsidiary lending depends on i4B's performance — the paper does not explain why the additional capital is needed or what it finances.
findings.matters: Borrowing to lend to subsidiaries multiplies risk if the subsidiary underperforms or if the housing market slows. A lender needs to know if i4B is struggling (needing rescue capital) or thriving (expansion investment).
findings.figures: i4B Holdings Ltd Subsidiary Loans: £179.2m (2025/26) → £211.2m (2026/27). Total service investments funded by borrowing: £326.4m (2026/27).
findings.quote: i4B Holdings Ltd Subsidiary Loans* 179.2 211.2... *new £32m capital loan included in 2026/27 onwards

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Capital programme 65% delivered with £102.3m slippage; Invest for Brent £40m facility not drawn
findings.detail: The capital programme delivered £215.4m against a revised budget of £328.9m (65% delivery rate). Slippage totaled £102.3m. Invest for Brent's £40m loan and equity facility for private rented sector acquisitions was not drawn in 2025/26 and is expected to draw in 2026/27, creating timing and delivery risk. Housing acquisition shortfalls: fewer properties acquired under LAHF and CHAPS than planned.
findings.matters: A slippage rate of 31% suggests delivery capacity constraints. The I4B delay (£40m) creates timing risk for 2026/27 cash flow. Housing acquisition shortfall is material given homelessness pressures; the council needs to acquire properties faster to create temporary accommodation supply, but is underperforming.
findings.figures: £215.4m actual vs £328.9m budget; £102.3m slippage; 65% delivery rate; I4B £40m undrawn; 7 of 15 LAHF/CHAPS properties targeted; 543 of 820 council homes delivered
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the Council delivered £209.7m capital expenditure against a revised capital budget of £328.9m. The variance consists of £16.8m net underspend and £102.3m slippage.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: HRA break-even achieved through one-off provision release (£2.6m) and asset disposal (£3.1m); structural repairs backlog mounting
findings.detail: The HRA reported break-even, but underlying pressures are substantial and growing. Repairs and maintenance overspent by £8.5m (£25.9m actual vs £17.4m budget), driven by high volumes of complex repairs, damp and mould cases, and new Awaab's Law compliance obligations from October 2025 (expanding further October 2026). Break-even was achieved via a £2.6m provision release (leaseholder debt no longer required) and £3.1m gain on asset disposals—neither repeatable.
findings.matters: One-off items mask structural deficit. Repairs costs are real and structural; the council has self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing (C3 grading) and Awaab's Law compliance will expand, both signaling the repairs backlog is a medium-term liability. A genuine underlying deficit may emerge once one-offs are exhausted.
findings.figures: Repairs £25.9m vs £17.4m budget (£8.5m overspend); break-even achieved by £2.6m provision release + £3.1m asset disposal; interest payable £14.0m (£2.0m above budget)
findings.quote: The movement on the allowance for bad or doubtful debts was a £2.6m credit, against a budgeted £1.4m charge – a £4.0m favourable variance. This arises from the release of a provision previously held against leaseholder service charge debt that is no longer required.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council Tax collection 91.6%, below target; long-term collection trajectory at risk from low in-year rates
findings.detail: In-year Council Tax collection was 91.6%, below the 92.5% target and only 0.4 percentage points above 2024/25 despite the service receiving investment post-review. The council's long-term collection target is 97%, but it explicitly states 'continued low in-year collection of Council Tax is a key risk to the Council's financial resilience in the medium term.' Working-age Council Tax Support recipients are paying at only 78%, with collection via benefits deductions proceeding 'slowly'.
findings.matters: Collection rates below target signal service underperformance. More critically, debt becomes 'much harder to collect after two years have passed', so the council's reliance on a 97% long-term rate is fragile if in-year collection stays at 91.6%. Future cash flow risk.
findings.figures: 91.6% in-year collection (vs 92.5% target); 0.4pp improvement vs 2024/25; long-term target 97%; CTS recipients 78% collection rate; 69% of CTS recipients have made a payment
findings.quote: Evidence suggests that debt becomes much harder to collect after two years have passed, so the continued low in-year collection of Council Tax is a key risk to the Council's financial resilience in the medium term.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Quarter 4 Purchase Order review uncovered £2.6m expenditure missed in prior forecasts; control weaknesses identified
findings.detail: Strategic Commissioning & Capacity Building overspent by £2.9m, with £2.6m of that arising from undiscovered expenditure identified only in Quarter 4. The review 'highlighted weaknesses in the end-to-end Purchase Order process, particularly around reconciliation and the timely reflection of commitments within financial forecasts.' A new Market Sustainability and Oversight Board has been established to prevent recurrence.
findings.matters: Hidden expenditure represents a control gap. The council did not see £2.6m of committed spend until year-end closedown. While corrected in the outturn, this signals risk that larger issues could go undetected in-year. The Board is newly established and untested.
findings.figures: £2.9m total overspend; £2.6m from undiscovered Purchase Orders; £2.6m primarily on Extra Care placements
findings.quote: During Quarter 4, a detailed review of Purchase Orders was undertaken. This exercise identified expenditure that had not been captured in previous forecasts, resulting in a large adjustment to the year-end position. The findings highlighted weaknesses in the end-to-end Purchase Order process, particularly around reconciliation and the timely reflection of commitments within financial forecasts.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reached £20.2m; High Needs Block up £8.2m in-year with 10.6% rise in EHCPs
findings.detail: The 2025/26 DSG deficit was £6.6m (£1.8m worse than Q3 forecast). The cumulative DSG deficit is now £20.2m, up from £13.6m at end of 2024/25. High Needs Block overspent by £8.2m, driven by a 10.6% increase in EHCPs (Education, Health and Care Plans) from 3,892 to 4,306. This deficit is ring-fenced in an 'unusable reserve' and cannot be funded from General Fund without Secretary of State approval.
findings.matters: SEND demand is rising structurally (10.6% increase in one year) and is unfunded. The cumulative deficit cannot be erased by council savings and represents a long-term structural liability. This is a national policy issue but a council balance sheet problem.
findings.figures: £6.6m in-year deficit; £20.2m cumulative deficit (vs £13.6m previous year); High Needs overspend £8.2m; EHCPs up 10.6% (3,892 to 4,306); funding blocks: Schools £0.4m underspend, Early Years £1.0m underspend
findings.quote: The HN Block reported an overspend of £8.2m compared to £4.8m reported in Quarter 3. The increase in overspend is primarily driven by increase in the top-up funding for children placed in special schools and academies due to an increase in pupil numbers. There was an increase in the number of children requiring Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) which was 4,306 as at March 2026 compared to 3,892 as at March 2025, an increase of 10.6%.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Homelessness support applications surged 40% to 8,795 in year; £11.7m overspend with 'no sustained stabilisation'
findings.detail: Housing Needs and Support overspent by £11.7m, a £7.2m deterioration from Q3. Applications totaled 8,795 by year-end (169 per week), a 40% increase from 6,281 in March 2025. Households in nightly paid accommodation rose from 1,182 (April 2025) to 1,428 (April 2026). The paper states demand 'has risen significantly beyond expectations' and notes 'no sustained stabilisation', with the pressure identified as 'the most significant financial pressure within the department.'
findings.matters: This is the single largest departmental overspend and is accelerating. The paper explicitly states there is 'no sustained stabilisation', meaning the council should expect continued deficits. This is structural (driven by Section 21 evictions and housing market failure) rather than operational, and will crowd out other services.
findings.figures: £11.7m overspend; £7.2m worse than Q3; 8,795 applications (40% increase vs March 2025, 6,281); 169 new applications per week; 1,428 households in nightly accommodation (+9% vs December 2025)
findings.quote: An initial £5m pressure was identified in Quarter 2, with limited movement at Quarter 3, followed by a sharper increase in demand and costs between November and March. This reflects continued growth in Stage 1 Temporary Accommodation demand, with no sustained stabilisation.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Adult Social Care £7.0m overspend with £1.3m of planned £4.8m savings unachieved; placement costs escalating sharply
findings.detail: Adult social care overspent by £7.0m. Homecare hours rose 3.4% while complexity drove steep cost uplifts: Residential Dementia placements up 40.1%, Nursing Dementia up 10.9%. Of £4.8m in required savings, £1.3m remain unachieved, including housing support contracts (£0.5m), Telecare charging (£0.4m), and reablement expansion (£0.2m). The paper states these shortfalls 'reflect both the intensity of demand led pressures and the impact of market driven cost inflation.'
findings.matters: Adult social care is demand-led and driven by demography and provider markets beyond council control. Unachieved savings and placement cost escalation (40%+ for dementia care) signal the budget is becoming unmanageable. The Cabinet Member frames this as a national funding failure, not a council failure, but the council must still find money.
findings.figures: £7.0m overspend; £1.3m savings unachieved; Residential Dementia up 40.1%; Nursing Dementia up 10.9%; Homecare hours up 3.4%; new placement costs up 26%+
findings.quote: Of the £4.8m savings required for the year, £1.3m remain unachieved. findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: General Fund £18.3m overspend funded from reserves, with Cabinet stating risks are 'essential' to manage in 2026/27

findings.matters: One-off reserve draws can only continue if demand pressures abate. The Cabinet Member's language suggests the council expects them to persist, meaning 2026/27 may require either further reserve draws or material service reductions.
findings.figures: £18.3m overspend; £5.8m worse than Q3 forecast; £16.7m drawn from Future Funding Risks reserve to balance budget

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Highway liability claims spiked from negligible to £1+ million in 2016 and remained elevated through 2022, suggesting underlying asset maintenance or infrastructure condition problems

findings.matters: The sustained elevation in liability payouts from 2016–2022 reflects real infrastructure problems that cost the council substantially; if the underlying maintenance backlog was not addressed, future liabilities could return to those levels.

findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the council has limited further room for conventional efficiency savings and future savings must come from service reduction or transformation

findings.matters: Transport costs for SEND are constrained by policy on EHCP eligibility (growing) but costs driven by wage inflation and asset replacement, limiting mitigation options
findings.figures: London Living Wage pressure £300k from April 2026

findings.quote: This reflects that collection remains lower than before the Covid-19 pandemic, representing a key risk to the MTFS.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Business Rates pooling arrangement ended; Brent now single authority operating with reset baseline and transitional safety net expiring
findings.detail: Brent exited the Eight Authority Business Rates Pool at end of 2025/26 after changes to the levy system removed the incentive to pool. The council now operates as a single authority. findings.headline: Prudential borrowing has increased from £659.1 million five years ago to £1,074.1 million and is forecast to rise to £1,274.6 million by March 2029

findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the trajectory of borrowing and the council's exposure to further interest rate shocks, particularly given the structural budget gaps
findings.figures: Borrowing at March 2026: £1,074.1m (up from £659.1m five years prior); forecast to reach £1,274.6m by March 2029

The issue reflects a national concern: providers are not bound by Local Housing Allowance caps and may charge higher rents by demonstrating support services, creating cost control challenges.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable cost pressures in a regulatory grey area create ongoing budget risk and may foreshadow similar pressures across other councils in this area
findings.figures: £2.1m overspend 2025/26
findings.quote: Historically managed within central corporate budgets, this area saw a £2.1m overspend in 2025/26 and remains under close scrutiny.

findings.matters: Double pressure in 2027/28 (rebuilding reserves plus closing budget gap) could force more aggressive savings or service reductions than currently planned

findings.quote: Based on the Quarter 1 forecast, without mitigation the Council would be required to utilise part of the General Fund balance to balance the 2026/27 budget.

findings.detail: The council delivered £209.8m of capital expenditure against a revised budget of £328.9m, representing 65% delivery. The programme reported £119.1m of underspending 'largely due to project slippage and rephasing of expenditure across affordable housing, South Kilburn regeneration, corporate assets and housing schemes'. The report states 'Most of the variance is expected to be carried forward into future years', but the scale of slippage raises delivery risk on the council's £1.25bn five-year investment programme.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage is common but concerning when a council is relying on capital-led growth (housing, regeneration) to improve medium-term financial sustainability. Consistent underspend suggests either weak project management or over-ambition in planning.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee

findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumes delivery of £10.4m savings agreed by Full Council in February 2026. The council is using a 'new collaborative approach' focused on 'high-impact opportunities, including cross-directorate working, improving productivity, better use of digital solutions, and increasing income generation'. However, the children's directorate has £0.4m of its £1.6m savings target flagged as at risk, and the report notes that 'a small number of proposals remain subject to delivery risk'. Given the £9.5m current overspend, successful delivery of these savings is essential.
findings.matters: The council is budgeting to break even on savings that have not yet been delivered and carry delivery risk. If savings slip, the council will overspend again and further deplete reserves. Lenders need confidence in the robustness of savings plans.

findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Outlook forecasts a cumulative budget gap of approximately £50m by 2031/32. The gap is 'driven primarily by the increasing cost of maintaining existing statutory services rather than the introduction of new services', reflecting that homelessness, adult social care, children's social care and SEND are consuming budget growth. The council has already delivered £248m of savings since 2010, limiting further scope for traditional spending reductions.
findings.matters: A £50m unfunded gap over five years indicates the council's baseline revenue is insufficient to meet statutory service costs as currently demanded. With savings already heavily drawn, future sustainability depends on transformation and capital-led growth, which are uncertain.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £7.0m in 2025/26 from demand and complexity exceeding budget growth assumptions
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £7.0m in 2025/26 as a result of 'increasing demand, rising complexity of need, higher placement costs and market inflation, particularly within residential, nursing and supported living services'. The budget had included growth to address rising demand, but 'activity levels and complexity exceeded expectations'. This is a structural recurring pressure.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is demographic and unlikely to reverse. An overspend this large despite deliberate budget growth suggests the council's modelling of care costs and demand is consistently insufficient, indicating further pressure ahead as the elderly population grows.

findings.paper_title: 7. Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy Cover Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit growing to £38.4m by end of 2026/27, driven by growing number of Education, Health and Care Plans
findings.detail: The DSG recorded a £6.6m deficit in 2025/26 (£1.8m worse than Q3 forecast), and is now forecasting an in-year deficit of £18.2m in 2026/27. The pressure is driven by continuing growth in the number of children with EHCPs, increasing demand for specialist provision and rising placement costs. Although government support has been announced to fund 90% of historic deficits accrued up to March 2026, the report makes clear this 'does not address the ongoing structural imbalance between funding and demand'.
findings.matters: A £38.4m cumulative deficit in a ringfenced grant that does not carry forward is a major financial stability risk. The council cannot legally cover this from general reserves indefinitely, and the structural nature of the gap (demand outpacing funding) signals ongoing exposure.

findings.detail: Housing Needs and Support overspent by £11.7m in 2025/26, driven by 8,795 homelessness applications and 1,428 households in nightly-paid temporary accommodation by April 2026. findings.detail: The council overspent its revenue budget by £18.3m in 2025/26—an adverse movement of £5.8m from the Quarter 3 forecast—and funded this entirely from earmarked reserves. Each 0.1% reduction results in approximately £0.2m loss of resources.

findings.detail: Looked After Children (LAC) residential placements increased from 32 full-time equivalents in 2022/23 to 47 in 2025/26. Individual high-need placements cost up to £0.5m per annum, with the most expensive recorded at £15k per week. The current 2026/27 forecast assumes a break-even position but this is volatile given the demand-led nature. In a worst-case scenario there could be an overspend of up to £3.2m; in a best case, an underspend of £1.4m. New placements are 14-16% more expensive than those they replace.
findings.matters: Placement costs are demand-driven and largely outside the council's control (court-ordered remand placements are unavoidable). The acceleration from 32 to 47 placements in four years shows worsening complexity in the cohort, not just volume.
findings.figures: Residential placements: 32 (2022/23) to 47 (2025/26); worst-case overspend £3.2m; most expensive placement £15k/week
findings.quote: The reliance on high-cost placements, combined with a limited supply of affordable alternatives, continues to exert sustained pressure on the budget.

findings.headline: Homelessness spending overshot by £11.7m in 2025/26 and is now expected to exceed the expanded 2026/27 budget by up to a further £5m.
findings.detail: The Housing Needs and Support budget overspent by £11.7m in 2025/26, forcing the council to increase the 2026/27 budget by £8m. Despite this, officers now report that average nightly-paid accommodation costs have risen by around £10 per night per placement. Based on current activity levels, this could result in expenditure being up to £5m higher than initially anticipated for 2026/27. Homelessness applications reached 8,795 by end of 2025/26 (169 new applications per week), and households in nightly accommodation rose from 1,182 (April 2025) to 1,428 (April 2026).
findings.matters: This is an ongoing demand-led overspend on a material service. The council has admitted savings plans from previous years have not landed ('the financial position of the Council has worsened since the February budget report'), and homelessness costs continue to accelerate beyond budget projections.
findings.figures: £11.7m overspend 2025/26; £8m budget increase 2026/27; potential additional £5m overspend 2026/27; 1,428 households in nightly accommodation (9% increase on year)
findings.quote: more recent information suggests average costs have risen by around £10 a night per placement. Based on current activity levels, this could result in expenditure being up to £5m higher than initially anticipated for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £50m over the next five years with no identified savings source beyond 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council faces a £5m gap in 2027/28, rising to £15m in 2028/29, then £10m per annum to 2031/32. At the time the budget was agreed in February 2026, no specific savings had been identified in respect of 2027/28 or 2028/29. The gap covers the cost of maintaining existing statutory provision in the face of inflation and demographic change, largely driven by demand pressures in social care and homelessness which the council says it has limited ability to control.
findings.matters: A £50m cumulative shortfall is material to the council's rating. The front-loading of government grant means the gap widens after 2028/29, and funding beyond then is uncertain pending the next Spending Review.
findings.quote: Current modelling identifies a cumulative budget gap of around £50 million between 2027/28 and 2031/32.

findings.headline: Phase 2 (Adult Education and Community Building) is unfunded and will require separate capital approval; total Bridge Park scheme cost still unknown.
findings.detail: The 2019 £50m budget was intended to cover both phases. Phase 1 is now £53.50m. Phase 2 scope and cost are not included in this paper; it will be presented separately.
findings.matters: Full regeneration scheme cost unknown; Phase 2 funding will require additional approval and may face similar budget pressures.
findings.figures: Phase 1 capital budget £53.50m; Phase 2 budget 'to follow in a separate report'
findings.quote: The budget request for Phase 2 will follow in a separate report.

findings.headline: Entire scheme contingent on planning approval and resolution of historic building listing appeals; DCMS appeal outcome still pending as of report date.
findings.detail: Buildings were candidates for listing; the Secretary of State decided not to list but an appeal has been lodged and DCMS has not confirmed outcome. Planning application submission target is October 2026. Conditional Land Sale Agreement is contingent on planning and financial viability.
findings.matters: Project delivery at risk if listing is overturned or planning refused; delays would extend vacant site holding costs.
findings.figures: Planning application submission October 2026; planning determination July 2027 (target); start on site April 2028
findings.quote: In January 2026, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) confirmed that an appeal had been lodged against these decisions and at the time of drafting this report, DCMS has not confirmed the outcome of this appeal and review.

findings.headline: Council currently spending ~£0.20m annually on vacant site security and business rates; costs continue until demolition and completion of Conditional Land Sale Agreement.
findings.detail: These are ongoing revenue costs with no end date specified, dependent on land sale completion and demolition timing.
findings.matters: Recurring unfunded cost not covered by project budget; timeline for elimination unclear.
findings.figures: £0.20m per annum current security costs, plus unquantified business rates
findings.quote: The current costs to secure the vacant Bridge Park Complex is approximately £0.20m per annum. There are also ongoing Business Rates liabilities for the council from the vacant site. These costs are expected to continue at least in part until such time that the demolition works take place, the CLSA completes and the part of the site being sold is no longer owned by the council.

findings.headline: £2.50m borrowing committed, creating £0.25m annual revenue charge dependent on leisure centre generating operational surplus.
findings.detail: At assumed 5% interest and 4% MRP, the annual cost is £0.25m. This is assumed to be covered by leisure centre management and operational surplus, supported by an independent commercial appraisal and benchmarking against Vale Farm Sports Centre.
findings.matters: Adds recurring revenue commitment; if the leisure centre does not deliver forecast surplus, creates budget pressure; no contingency stated.
findings.figures: £2.50m borrowing; £0.25m annual revenue cost (5% interest + 4% MRP)
findings.quote: Assuming interest costs of 5% and minimum revenue provision (a prudent charge for the repayment of borrowing) of 4%, this will result in annual cost to revenue budgets of £0.25m. This is anticipated to be covered by the management and operational surplus.

findings.headline: £39.0m of the £53.50m capital budget (78%) is funded from Strategic Community Infrastructure Levy, described as a significant allocation reducing flexibility for other projects.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges this concentration. There is sufficient SCIL available (£47.9m pipeline for wider Bridge Park/Hillside Corridor), but officers are exploring alternative sources including Sport England funding and increased land sale proceeds to reduce the SCIL requirement.
findings.matters: Reduces capital flexibility for other infrastructure projects; reliance on SCIL success and Sport England funding which is not assumed.
findings.figures: £39.0m SCIL of £50.0m total financing (excluding the £3.50m budget gap)
findings.quote: £39.0m is however a significant use of SCIL reducing the amount available for other projects. Therefore, officers are exploring alternative funding sources such as Sport England and potential increases in the capital receipt from the land sale.

findings.headline: Capital budget for Bridge Park Phase 1 increased to £53.50m, up from £50m approved in 2019 and covering Phase 1 only.
findings.detail: The 2019 budget was based on high-level feasibility and covered both phases. Better cost knowledge and construction inflation mean Phase 1 alone now costs £53.50m. A 10% contingency (£4.90m) is included. Phase 2 funding follows in a separate paper.
findings.matters: Significant scope creep on a major capital scheme; contingency may be inadequate in continuing inflation; Phase 2 costs unknown and unfunded.
findings.figures: £53.50m total Phase 1 budget (£50m originally approved in 2019 for both phases); construction £38.64m, fees £6.00m, contingency £4.90m
findings.quote: When Cabinet first approved a £50,000,000 budget for Bridge Park in 2019, the intention was for this to cover both Phase 1 and Phase 2. However, this report was based on a high-level feasibility assessment of the buildings and since this report, the requirements and constraints of the site and buildings are better known and so the costs to deliver the scheme have increased.

findings.headline: Financing cost affordability improved to 9.0% of revenue in 2025/26 but depends on achieving 32% revenue growth by 2028/29
findings.detail: The proportion of net revenue consumed by financing costs fell from 10.8% (2024/25 actual) to 9.0% (2025/26 actual), with forecasts to 7.4% by 2028/29. Absolute financing costs remain stable at £38-42m annually, but the improving ratio assumes the revenue stream grows from £431m to £569m. If revenue growth does not materialize as forecast, the affordability position could deteriorate rapidly.
findings.matters: Affordability ratios signal debt sustainability. While the 2025/26 outturn improvement is positive, it is heavily dependent on revenue assumptions (population growth, business rates, government funding). A shortfall in revenue growth would quickly reverse gains and strain repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Proportion of net revenue stream: 10.8% (2024/25) to 9.0% (2025/26) to 7.4% (2028/29 forecast); Net Revenue Stream £431.4m to £568.6m; Financing Costs £38.9m to £41.9m
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream (%) 10.8% 9.0% 8.3% 7.8% 7.4%

findings.headline: £287.5m of the council's £331m investment portfolio is funded by borrowing, with £223.1m concentrated in i4B Holdings subsidiary
findings.detail: Brent is financing substantial service investments through borrowing rather than from operational revenue. The largest exposure is i4B Holdings Ltd (a housing development subsidiary) at £179.2m in loans and £43.9m equity. First Wave Housing accounts for a further £33.4m. Unlike traditional infrastructure, these subsidiary investments carry operational risk if schemes underperform; the council must service the debt regardless of investment returns.
findings.matters: Concentration risk in subsidiary loans means the council's financial position depends on the performance of commercial housing schemes. If i4B or First Wave underperform, the council faces both revenue loss and mandatory debt service costs, affecting affordability.
findings.figures: Total Funded by Borrowing 287.5m; i4B Loans 179.2m; i4B Equity 51.9m; First Wave Housing 33.4m; Total Investments 331.3m
findings.quote: These investments are the loans to the Council's subsidiaries i4B Holdings Ltd and First Wave Housing Ltd.

findings.headline: Capital financing requirement has grown to £1,412m with projections to £1,636m by 2028/29
findings.detail: Brent's CFR increased from £1,354m (2024/25) to £1,412m (2025/26 actual), requiring external debt to rise from £900m to £1,074m. The council is executing a capital programme of £939m over five years across regeneration (£264m), housing (£269m), and schools (£87m). To accommodate this, the Authorised Limit has been increased from £1,700m to £1,800m for 2025/26+ and £2,000m for 2027/28+. No breaches of limits occurred.
findings.matters: Material debt accumulation over a short timeframe affects repayment capacity and may constrain future borrowing flexibility. Lenders need to assess whether the trajectory is sustainable.
findings.figures: CFR 1,354.5 to 1,635.8; External Loans 900.0 to 1,274.6; Authorised Limit increased to 1,800.0-2,000.0; Total capital expenditure 209.9m (2025/26 actual)
findings.quote: The Council has a significant borrowing requirement and balance and is therefore exposed to financial risks including the loss of invested funds and the revenue effect of changing interest rates.

findings.headline: Q3 forecast accuracy on major pressures deteriorated significantly, with homelessness overspend alone up £7.2m in final quarter
findings.detail: Between Q3 (January 2026 forecast) and year-end, the General Fund overspend worsened by £5.8m. The homelessness pressure alone increased by £7.2m in Q4. Adult Social Care improved by £1.7m (reclassification of prior-year costs) but this masks ongoing control issues. The pattern shows the council's forecasting is unreliable for volatile, demand-led services, particularly housing and social care.
findings.matters: A lender needs reliable quarterly forecasting to assess trajectory. A £5.8m adverse movement in one quarter (10% of the final overspend) suggests in-year monitoring is weak and cost trends are not being captured until they are unavoidable.
findings.figures: Q3 General Fund forecast overspend: £12.5m; actual overspend: £18.3m; adverse movement: £5.8m; Homelessness Q3 forecast: £4.5m; actual: £11.7m; adverse movement: £7.2m; Adult Social Care Q3 forecast: £8.7m; actual: £7.0m (improvement linked to reclassification, not management)
findings.quote: The General Fund recorded an overspend of £18.3m, representing an adverse movement of £5.8m compared with the Quarter 3 forecast reported to Cabinet in January 2026.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 65% of budget (£209.7m of £328.9m), with £40m Invest for Brent facility completely undrawn
findings.detail: The capital programme slipped by £102.3m (31% of revised budget). The entire £40m Invest for Brent loan and equity facility to I4B Holdings was undrawn and is expected to be drawn in 2026-27. The council cites "inherent complexity of delivering a large investment programme in a challenging operating environment," including constrained contractor market, procurement law changes, and late grant announcements. This is systemic delivery weakness, not isolated projects.
findings.matters: Capital slippage means planned investment and savings are not realised. A 35% underspend/slippage rate signals the council cannot execute its investment programme at the pace forecast. The undrawn I4B facility is particularly material—it was supposed to finance acquisitions to provide temporary accommodation, which is exactly where the council has a £11.7m pressure.
findings.figures: Total capital outturn £209.7m vs revised budget £328.9m (65% delivery); slippage £102.3m; Invest for Brent £40m undrawn; capital delivered by area: Housing GF £50.1m vs £73.9m; Regeneration £73.5m vs £84.2m; Public Realm £22.9m vs £34.9m
findings.quote: The level of slippage across the 2025/26 Capital Programme reflects the inherent complexity of delivering a large investment programme in a challenging operating environment. Ambitious NCIL and SCIL schemes received Cabinet approval later in the financial year, compressing the time available for delivery.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection remained below target at 91.6%, with working-age CTS recipients collecting at only 78%
findings.detail: In-year Council Tax collection was 91.6%, below the 92.5% target. The council attributes weakness to the new Council Tax Support scheme introduced April 2025, which requires working-age CTS recipients to pay a minimum 35%. Only 78% of working-age CTS recipients collected their 2025-26 bill, with 69% making any payment at all. The council notes that "debt becomes much harder to collect after two years have passed, so the continued low in-year collection of Council Tax is a key risk to the Council's financial resilience in the medium term."
findings.matters: Council Tax is a core, stable income source. Falling collection rates signal either economic stress among residents or council collection weakness. The specific weakness in CTS working-age recipients suggests the policy change (35% minimum payment) is creating non-paying cohorts. The council's own warning about medium-term resilience risk is significant.
findings.figures: In-year collection 91.6% vs 92.5% target; working-age CTS collection rate 78%; 69% of working-age CTS recipients made any payment; net collectable amount £238.7m
findings.quote: Evidence suggests that debt becomes much harder to collect after two years have passed, so the continued low in-year collection of Council Tax is a key risk to the Council's financial resilience in the medium term.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account repairs budget overran by £8.5m (49%) due to complexity and new legal obligations from Awaab's Law
findings.detail: HRA repairs and maintenance outturn was £25.9m against a budget of £17.4m. The budget was set below prior-year outturn (£21.4m in 2024-25), understating actual demand. The council identified high volumes of complex repairs, damp and mould cases, and transition to new service contracts. Awaab's Law (came into force 27 October 2025) introduces new statutory obligations to remediate hazards within specified timescales, which will increase costs further.
findings.matters: Housing stock repairs are a fixed cost that must be paid. A £8.5m overspend in one year signals the council is not adequately funding the stock condition needs, and the legal obligation introduced by Awaab's Law will lock in higher spend for years. This is pressure on HRA cash flow.
findings.figures: Repairs and maintenance: £25.9m actual vs £17.4m budget (£8.5m overspend, 49% over); 2024-25 actual £21.4m, showing budget was set below run-rate; new statutory obligations introduced October 2025
findings.quote: Demand for repairs and maintenance services remained significantly above budgeted levels. A high volume of complex repairs, an increase in damp and mould cases, and the transition to new service contracts placed sustained pressure on the budget, alongside the new statutory obligations introduced by Awaab's Law, which came into force for the social rented sector on 27 October 2025.

findings.headline: Strategic Commissioning identified unexplained expenditure commitments only at year-end, revealing financial control weaknesses
findings.detail: A detailed review of Purchase Orders in Q4 uncovered £2.6m in extra care placements and other expenditure that had not been captured in earlier forecasts. The council explicitly identified "weaknesses in the end-to-end Purchase Order process, particularly around reconciliation and the timely reflection of commitments within financial forecasts." Extra care was originally designed as a cost-effective alternative to residential care but now frequently matches or exceeds traditional care home costs.
findings.matters: A council discovering major expenditure commitments at year-end, rather than throughout the year, signals weak month-to-month financial control. This increases forecasting risk and suggests in-year forecasts are not reliable. The comment on extra care cost convergence shows the council is not getting expected savings from care redesign.
findings.figures: £2.6m pressure in Commissioning and Contracts identified late in year; £2.9m total Strategic Commissioning overspend; extra care costs now matching traditional care home costs
findings.quote: During Quarter 4, a detailed review of Purchase Orders was undertaken. This exercise identified expenditure that had not been captured in previous forecasts, resulting in a large adjustment to the year-end position. The findings highlighted weaknesses in the end-to-end Purchase Order process, particularly around reconciliation and the timely reflection of commitments within financial forecasts.

findings.headline: Reserve drawdown of £16.7m needed to balance the budget, using the Future Funding Risks reserve
findings.detail: The council drew £16.7m from its Future Funding Risks reserve in 2025-26 to meet its statutory obligation to balance the General Fund. This was necessary because service overspends (£18.3m) exceeded central funding movements (£2.1m surplus). The drawdown signals the council is not managing in-year pressures from its current budget envelope.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a key lender indicator. A council drawing on reserves to balance a budget is unsustainable and signals structural deficits. Future reserves will be smaller, leaving the council with less capacity to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: £16.7m drawn from Future Funding Risks reserve; General Fund overspend £18.3m; Central Funding net underspend £2.1m
findings.quote: To ensure that the Council met its statutory obligation to balance the General Fund revenue budget without adjusting the service area outturns, a drawdown of £16.7m from the Future Funding Risks reserve to Central Budgets was carried out.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit now £20.2m and growing, driven by a 10.6% surge in children requiring specialist education support
findings.detail: The High Needs Block (funding for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans) overspent by £8.2m in 2025-26, adding to a cumulative deficit that was already £13.6m. The number of children with EHCPs increased from 3,892 to 4,306 (10.6% growth). This is a ring-fenced deficit that cannot be funded from general reserves and must be carried forward and recovered from future funding, creating structural pressure on budgets for years.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are immovable: they cannot be balanced against the General Fund without Secretary of State approval. A growing deficit of £20.2m signals the council is unable to absorb growing SEN demand within its allocation, and this will consume future years' cash flow and constrain all other spending.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £20.2m (up from £13.6m); in-year deficit £6.6m; High Needs Block overspend £8.2m; EHCP numbers +10.6% (3,892 to 4,306); sustained top-up cost growth across special schools, academies, and independent placements
findings.quote: The increase in overspend is primarily driven by increase in the top-up funding for children placed in special schools and academies due to an increase in pupil numbers.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £7m driven by complexity-driven costs rising far beyond budget assumptions
findings.detail: Placement costs across adult social care are accelerating faster than the council budgeted for. Homecare hours up 3.4%; Residential Dementia placements up 40.1%; Nursing Dementia placements up 10.9%; Learning Disability supported living packages up 5.6% with weekly costs rising 9.5%. New spot-purchase residential care costs are rising over 26%. Despite budget growth, £1.3m of £4.8m planned savings remain unachieved because cost inflation outpaced the growth built into the 2025-26 budget.
findings.matters: This is structural demand-led pressure in a core statutory service that is ageing-population driven. The council cannot reduce this spending. A 40% cost rise in one category suggests market stress that may persist, and the council's inability to deliver planned savings signals forecasting weakness.
findings.figures: £7.0m overspend in Adult Social Care (improved from £8.7m forecast but still significant); Residential Dementia +40.1%; Nursing Dementia +10.9%; Learning Disability costs +9.5%; new residential placements +26%; £1.3m of £4.8m savings unachieved
findings.quote: activity levels and complexity exceeded expectations, resulting in overspends in these demand led areas... The scale of these cost increases, which exceed the growth assumptions built into the 2025/26 budget, has created significant challenges in delivering planned savings.

findings.headline: Homelessness applications surged 40% in a single year, creating an £11.7m overspend that exceeds budget expectations
findings.detail: Brent received 8,795 homelessness applications by end of 2025-26, up from 6,281 in March 2025. Households in nightly paid accommodation rose from 1,182 (April 2025) to 1,428 (April 2026). The overspend increased by £7.2m between Q3 and year-end, with demand rising "significantly beyond expectations" after November. The council notes this is the highest demand in their records, averaging 169 new applications per week.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a structural, demand-led cost that a council cannot refuse to provide. A lender needs to know this is not a one-year anomaly but a sustained shift, and the council is struggling to forecast and manage it.
findings.figures: 40% increase in applications (6,281 to 8,795); 9% increase in nightly accommodation (1,182 to 1,428); £11.7m overspend in Housing Needs and Support; demand increased "by approximately half of the annual increase occurring between Quarter 3 and Quarter 4"
findings.quote: An initial £5m pressure was identified in Quarter 2, with limited movement at Quarter 3, followed by a sharper increase in demand and costs between November and March. This reflects continued growth in Stage 1 Temporary Accommodation demand, with no sustained stabilisation.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement peaks at £1,827.9m in 2029/30, a 29% increase from current level
findings.detail: The council's CFR is forecast to rise from £1,412.3m (2025/26 actual) to £1,571.2m (2026/27) and peak at £1,827.9m in 2029/30 before declining slightly to £1,813.5m by 2030/31. This trajectory reflects the forward capital programme shown in section (a), with peaks in affordable housing and regeneration investment.
findings.matters: Sustained high debt levels sustained over the medium term; lenders need confidence that the council has a credible path to debt reduction after 2029/30, and that financing costs remain affordable given the rising revenue stream.

findings.headline: New £32m capital loan commitment to i4B Holdings subsidiary funded entirely by borrowing
findings.detail: The indicators reveal a new £32m capital loan to i4B Holdings Ltd commencing in 2026/27, in addition to existing loans of £179.2m (2025/26 actual). Total loans to i4B and First Wave Housing total £326.4m in 2026/27, all funded by the council's borrowing. These represent contingent liabilities if the subsidiaries underperform.
findings.matters: Material new commitment that increases council leverage; represents indirect exposure to subsidiary performance risk; part of the £75.8m YoY borrowing increase.
findings.figures: i4B Holdings loans £211.2m (including £32m new capital loan); First Wave Housing £32.9m; total service investments funded by borrowing £326.4m
findings.quote: *new £32m capital loan included in 2026/27 onwards

findings.headline: Capital expenditure and borrowing requirement rising 66% and 75% respectively in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's capital programme is jumping from £209.9m actual in 2025/26 to £348.0m estimated for 2026/27. The borrowing requirement rises correspondingly from £101.1m to £176.9m — a 75% increase. The major components are affordable housing (£67.3m), regeneration (£79.0m), and South Kilburn scheme (£60.5m).
findings.matters: A material acceleration in the council's borrowing profile; lenders need to understand whether this is sustainable and whether it reflects catch-up investment, policy expansion, or external pressure.
findings.figures: Capital Expenditure 2025/26 £209.9m → 2026/27 £348.0m; Borrowing £101.1m → £176.9m
findings.quote: Total Capital Expenditure 209.9 348.0 [and] Borrowing 101.1 176.9

findings.headline: All cash investments held in money market funds with 100% bail-in exposure, higher concentration risk than comparable authorities
findings.detail: Brent's £43.8m investment portfolio is held entirely in same-day access money market funds. This provides maximum liquidity but means 100% of investments are subject to bail-in risk if a financial institution fails, compared to 80% for similar London councils and 64% across all local authorities in the Arlingclose peer group. The paper acknowledges this but states the strategy prioritises liquidity over diversification.
findings.matters: Concentrated bail-in exposure creates contingent risk: if a major UK bank fails and triggers bail-in of local authority deposits, Brent would lose a material proportion of its liquid reserves. This is not hedged.
findings.figures: Money Market Funds £43.8m. Brent bail-in exposure 100% vs similar London councils 80% vs all local authorities 64%.
findings.quote: Whilst this highly liquid investment strategy provides maximum flexibility, it also means that 100% of Brent's investments remain subject to bail-in exposure, compared with 80% for similar London authorities and 64% across all Arlingclose local authority clients.

findings.headline: Non-treasury investments in council subsidiaries total £287.5m, with £179.2m loaned to i4B Holdings for purchase-to-let housing
findings.detail: The council has invested heavily in two wholly-owned subsidiaries: i4B Holdings (£179.2m in loans plus £43.9m equity) and First Wave Housing (£33.4m in loans). These investments are illiquid and dependent on residential property values and rental income. i4B converted £3.2m working capital into shares during the year. These investments generated £6.0m income.
findings.matters: Large subsidiary loans represent concentrated property market exposure. If rental income falls or property values decline, the council's ability to recover these loans is at risk. The paper does not assess property valuations or rental income adequacy.
findings.figures: i4B loans £179.2m, shareholdings £43.9m. First Wave Housing loans £33.4m. Total service investments £287.5m. Interest income £6.0m.
findings.quote: As of 31st March 2026, the Council had provided loan financing of £179.2m to i4B (£182.4m in 2024/25) which is secured against the company's properties.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing has halved from £453.8m to £338.2m, indicating the council is depleting its cash reserves to fund capital
findings.detail: Internal borrowing (using reserves and balances instead of external debt) fell by £115.6m during the year. This represents a strategy where the council chose to raise external debt (£295m new loans) rather than continue drawing down internal cash. The declining internal borrowing pool limits future flexibility.
findings.matters: Declining internal borrowing capacity means fewer tools to manage cash flow or refinance debt without market access. It also suggests the council may have fewer reserves to absorb unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £453.8m (31 March 2025) to £338.2m (31 March 2026). Decrease of £115.6m.
findings.quote: The difference between the Loan CFR and external loans is internal borrowing... The Council's internal borrowing (Loans CFR less external borrowing) reduced from £453.8m to £338.2m.

findings.headline: New borrowing costs more than legacy portfolio, pushing average interest rate up to 3.9% and locking in higher future debt service
findings.detail: The average interest rate on external borrowing increased from 3.85% to 3.90% despite Bank Rate falling during the year. This marginal increase occurred because new PWLB borrowing was undertaken at rates (5.38% to 5.72% for 10-year loans) significantly higher than the existing portfolio average. This effect will persist as the legacy portfolio of lower-rate debt matures.
findings.matters: A rising average cost of debt reduces financial flexibility and makes the council's capital programme more expensive to finance. This is particularly concerning if capital spending continues at current levels.
findings.figures: Average borrowing rate 3.85% (31 March 2025) to 3.90% (31 March 2026). PWLB 10-year rates ranged 5.38% to 5.72%.
findings.quote: The average interest rate on the Council's external borrowing increased marginally from 3.85% at 31 March 2025 to 3.90% at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Two LOBO loans totalling £20m were forced to refinance at rates of 6.24% and 6.41% after lender rate increases, signalling refinancing risk
findings.detail: LOBO loans give lenders the option to increase rates at specified dates. In 2025/26, two LOBO loans (both from Dexia) were called when rates were hiked to 6.24% and 6.41%. The council chose to repay rather than accept the higher rates, requiring refinancing through PWLB. One remaining LOBO of £9.5m faces a rate review in 2026/27.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create contingent refinancing risk that cannot be controlled by the borrower. The substantial rate increases (from 4.1% and 5.2% to 6.24% and 6.41%) demonstrate market stress. Another £9.5m is at risk in the coming year.
findings.figures: £10.0m Dexia loan at 4.1% repriced to 6.41%. £10.0m Dexia loan at 5.2% repriced to 6.24%. Remaining LOBO exposure £9.5m due for review 2026/27.
findings.quote: The council repaid two LOBO loans in 2025/26 after the lender exercised their option... Loan 1 - Dexia £10.0m at 4.1% repriced to 6.41%. Loan 2 - Dexia £10.0m at 5.2% repriced to 6.24%.

findings.headline: Working capital increased by £70m due to rising debtors, while cash investments fell, indicating potential liquidity stress
findings.detail: Working capital jumped from £89.6m to £159.2m, driven primarily by a £70m increase in debtors (amounts owed to the council), partially offset by £10m reduction in creditors. Despite this increase in accounting working capital, actual cash investments fell from £47.3m to £43.8m. The paper notes that timing of debtor receipt influences cash flow and can require short-term borrowing.
findings.matters: Growing debtors represent cash owed but not yet collected. If collection slows or defaults rise, this creates liquidity pressure. The council is investing more cash in capital while waiting for debtors to pay, which may force additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Working capital increased from £89.6m to £159.2m. Debtors increased by approximately £70m. Money Market Funds fell from £47.3m to £43.8m.
findings.quote: In addition, working capital increased from £89.6m at 31 March 2025 to £159.2m at 31 March 2026, primarily due to a £70m increase in debtors during the year.

findings.headline: Net borrowing position deteriorated sharply to £1,030m as cash reserves declined faster than debtors were collected
findings.detail: Net borrowing (debt minus cash investments) worsened by £177.6m during the year, from £852.7m to £1,030.3m. This occurred despite Capital Financing Requirement being managed through Minimum Revenue Provision charges of £16.5m. The deterioration reflects both new borrowing for capital and declining cash balances.
findings.matters: Net borrowing position is a key indicator of financial leverage and refinancing risk. A deteriorating position indicates the council is becoming increasingly dependent on debt financing rather than internal resources.
findings.figures: Net borrowing £852.7m (31 March 2025) to £1,030.3m (31 March 2026). Change of £177.6m.
findings.quote: As a result, the Council's net borrowing position (less investments) changed from £852.7m to £1,030.3m.

findings.headline: Borrowing increased by £174m in a single year to fund capital programme, raising total debt to £1,074m
findings.detail: The Council raised £295m of new loans during 2025/26, primarily through PWLB (£230m on Equal Instalment Principal basis), while repaying £121m. External borrowing rose from £900m to £1,074.1m. The bulk of new borrowing was PWLB loans structured to repay progressively over the loan term rather than maturity loans, which the council judged would lock in higher long-term costs.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk needs to understand the velocity of borrowing growth and whether it is sustainable. A £174m increase in annual borrowing for capital is material and signals confidence in the council's capital programme delivery.
findings.figures: £1,074.0m borrowing at 31 March 2026 vs £900.0m at 31 March 2025. New loans £295.0m, repaid loans £121.0m. PWLB new borrowing £230.0m.
findings.quote: Borrowing at 31 March 2026 was £1,074.0m an increase of £174.0m compared to 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Southwark Council exiting Shared Technology Services partnership by 31 March 2028, implications for Brent under review
findings.detail: Southwark Council has formally issued notice to exit the Shared Technology Services partnership, with completion targeted for 31 March 2028. A programme has commenced to plan Southwark's exit and to review implications for remaining partners including Brent. The financial impact on Brent has not yet been quantified in this document.
findings.matters: Shared services arrangements often involve cost-sharing and economies of scale. The exit of a major partner may increase costs for remaining councils or require restructuring. The implications are currently unquantified.
findings.figures: Completion date 31 March 2028
findings.quote: In January 2026 Southwark Council formally issued its notice to exit the Shared Technology Services partnership. The intended completion date for this is 31st March 2028. A programme has commenced to plan and coordinate Southwark's exit, and to also review the implications for the remaining partners, including Brent.

findings.headline: Planning fee income under pressure from Building Safety Regulator changes and development slowdown
findings.detail: Income from planning fees, including Building Control, is facing 'increasing financial risk'. Changes from the Building Safety Regulator have 'significantly reduced the Council's ability to bid for major schemes, with referral levels remaining low'. There is also a 'wider slowdown in development activity across the Borough'.
