Additionally, there is a 'workforce risk, as a high proportion of experienced staff are approaching retirement age; loss of capacity would directly reduce the ability to deliver services and generate income, creating a risk of further income shortfalls'. The council notes these factors 'represent a risk to the service's financial sustainability, with limited scope to mitigate through income growth alone'.
findings.matters: Planning fees are a discretionary income source that cannot be budgeted for with certainty. Regulatory and market changes outside the council's control are reducing this income. Combined with staffing risk, the council may not be able to recover this income.
findings.figures: Referral levels low; income recovery constrained; high proportion of experienced staff approaching retirement
findings.quote: These factors represent a risk to the service's financial sustainability, with limited scope to mitigate through income growth alone unless budget assumptions are realigned to reflect these ongoing constraints.

findings.headline: Council Tax income dependent on 4.99% annual increase; each 1% shortfall costs £2m plus cumulative impact
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes Council Tax increases of 4.99% per annum through the forecast period to offset funding pressures. For each 1% below the referendum limit in 2027/28, the council loses approximately £2m of funding. If a 1% lower increase were applied in both 2027/28 and 2028/29, the cumulative funding loss across the five-year period would be £20m. The council must also achieve tax base growth of 1.7% annually, but government assumptions in the settlement were higher, creating a mismatch of £1.5m (2026/27) rising to £5.3m (2028/29).
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on Council Tax precept increases creates political risk. If inflation moderates or public resistance increases, the council loses revenue with no offsetting savings plan in place. The tax base growth assumption may not be achieved given economic conditions.
findings.figures: 4.99% pa assumed increase; £2m loss per 1% shortfall in 2027/28; £20m cumulative loss if lower increase in both 2027/28 and 2028/29; tax base growth assumption 1.7% pa vs government settlement assumption creating £5.3m gap by 2028/29
findings.quote: For each 1% that Council Tax is increased by below the referendum limit, the Council loses c.£2m of funding as of 2027/28...a 1% lower Council Tax increase applied in 2027/28 would result in a relative reduction of the Council's funding by £2.5m in 2031/32 and the cumulative reduction in funding across the five year period would be £11m.

findings.headline: Funding uncertainty beyond 2028/29 with next Spending Review expected to constrain local government allocations
findings.detail: The multi-year local government finance settlement provides certainty only through 2028/29. Beyond this, the MTFS assumes modest increases but notes 'significant uncertainty regarding funding from 2029/30 onwards'. The next Spending Review will determine future funding in an environment where 'government departments [will be pressured] to reduce expenditure to fund increased commitments, particularly in areas such as defence and health'. The council assumes modest increases but this may not materialise.
findings.matters: Three years of visibility on funding is short. If the Spending Review produces flat or reducing allocations while demand pressures continue, the council will face even larger budget gaps than the current £50m projection.
findings.figures: Settlement certainty to 2028/29 only; £50m gap assumes modest future increases
findings.quote: At present it is not known what the funding environment for local government will be beyond 2028/29...Therefore, the most likely scenario is that any increases to funding for local authorities at that time will be modest.

findings.headline: Supported exempt accommodation overspend of £2.1m in 2025/26 with unresolved regulatory framework
findings.detail: Supported exempt accommodation saw a £2.1m overspend in 2025/26 and remains under close scrutiny. Providers are not bound by Local Housing Allowance caps and can charge higher rents by demonstrating support services. Housing Benefit subsidy levels are determined by Rent Officer assessments, making cost management difficult. The council notes this reflects a national concern highlighting the need for 'clearer regulatory frameworks and consistent criteria'. New regulatory requirements from the Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023 require councils to develop a local supported housing strategy by end of 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost issue where providers have pricing power and the council has limited levers to control costs. The uncertain regulatory environment means costs could increase further before controls are established.
findings.figures: £2.1m overspend in 2025/26; historically managed within central corporate budgets
findings.quote: Providers in this sector are not bound by LHA caps and may charge higher rents by demonstrating the provision of support services...This issue reflects a national concern, highlighting the need for clearer regulatory frameworks and consistent criteria.

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing increased 63% to £1,074.1m in five years, forecast to reach £1,274.6m by March 2029
findings.detail: The council's prudential borrowing has risen from £659.1m in March 2021 to £1,074.1m at March 2026, an increase of 63%. Borrowing is forecast to increase further to £1,274.6m by 31 March 2029. The council is highly exposed to interest rate shocks, with interest costs on prudential borrowing being the biggest driver of capital financing outturn. The council has built £3m growth into the 2026/27 budget to manage interest rate pressures. The council acknowledges that 'wider global factors' have 'placed pressure on the Council's medium term financial outlook' through interest rate increases.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing with higher interest rates significantly increases revenue pressure. The council's sensitivity to interest rate movements is substantial and difficult to forecast. Any further rate increases would force budget reductions elsewhere.
findings.figures: £1,074.1m prudential borrowing March 2026 (up from £659.1m in 2021); Forecast £1,274.6m by March 2029; £3m growth in 2026/27 budget for interest rate pressure
findings.quote: The Council's exposure to interest rate risk has increased in recent years because prudential borrowing has increased to £1,074.1m at 31 March 2026 compared to £659.1m five years earlier...Further global events or other interest rate shocks would place severe pressure on revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care showing volatile placement demand with financial risks of £3-3.5m each
findings.detail: Adult social care is forecasting breakeven but faces a potential financial risk of up to £3.5m if complex care demand is not effectively managed. New adult social care placements are 14-16% more expensive than those ending. Children's social care residential placements have increased from 32 FTE in 2022/23 to 47 in 2025/26, with individual placements exceeding £0.5m per annum and the most expensive reaching £15k per week. The current forecast is breakeven but the worst-case scenario shows an overspend of £3.2m.
findings.matters: These are demand-led, statutory services where the council has limited discretion. Volatility in placement numbers and complexity creates revenue budget uncertainty. The shift to higher-cost complex placements is a trend not a one-off.
findings.figures: Up to £3.5m risk in adult social care; Up to £3.2m worst-case overspend in children's social care; Residential placements up from 32 to 47 FTE; New placements 14-16% more expensive; Individual placements up to £15k/week
findings.quote: new placements typically 14-16% more expensive than those ending in the previous year. At Quarter 1, demand trends indicate a shift in placement types...This creates a potential financial risk of up to £3.5m if not effectively managed.

findings.headline: Homelessness/housing crisis driving £11.7m overspend in 2025/26 with further pressures emerging
findings.detail: Housing Needs and Support overspent by £11.7m in 2025/26, the budget was increased by £8m for 2026/27, yet the council now faces provider cost inflation of approximately £10/night per placement more than anticipated. This could result in expenditure being up to £5m higher than initially budgeted for 2026/27. The council received 8,795 homelessness applications in 2025/26 (169 per week), with 1,428 households in nightly paid accommodation in April 2026, up 9% since December 2025. Benchmarking shows Brent experienced an 85% rise in homelessness net expenditure between 2024/25 and 2025/26.
findings.matters: Homelessness is the single largest financial pressure and the council has limited control over demand. Even after a £8m budget increase, the service is tracking to further overspend. This is a structural cost pressure that will persist and could force reductions in other services.
findings.figures: £11.7m overspend 2025/26; £8m budget increase 2026/27; up to £5m additional pressure emerging; 8,795 applications in 2025/26; 1,428 households in nightly accommodation April 2026; 85% rise in net expenditure 2024/25-2025/26
findings.quote: more recent information suggests average costs have risen by around £10 a night per placement. Based on current activity levels, this could result in expenditure being up to £5m higher than initially anticipated for 2026/27.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves at adequacy level with risk of further depletion in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council drew down £16.7m from earmarked reserves in 2025/26 to cover overspends, leaving £24.3m of generally usable reserves. The General Fund Balance stands at £20.7m, representing the section 151 officer's assessment of adequate reserves (5% of net revenue budget). Without mitigation, the council would be forced to use part of the General Fund balance to balance the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Reserves at minimum adequacy levels provide limited buffer for unexpected pressures. Any further drawdown would leave the council with below-minimum reserves and require replenishment from future budgets, competing with other spending needs.
findings.figures: £24.3m generally usable reserves; £20.7m General Fund Balance; £16.7m drawdown in 2025/26; 5% adequacy requirement
findings.quote: Based on the Quarter 1 forecast, without mitigation the Council would be required to utilise part of the General Fund balance to balance the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £50m facing the council between 2027/28 and 2031/32
findings.detail: The council faces an in-year budget gap of £5m in 2027/28, rising to £15m in 2028/29, then £10m annually through 2031/32. This totals approximately £50m across the five-year MTFS period. The council has already made £248m of cuts since 2010, equivalent to almost half of the current net revenue budget.
findings.matters: This indicates structural budget pressures that cannot be solved through one-off measures. The council will need to find substantial recurring savings or increase revenues while maintaining service quality.
findings.figures: £50m cumulative gap 2027/28-2031/32; £248m cuts since 2010; £10.4m savings required in 2026/27
findings.quote: Current modelling identifies a cumulative budget gap of around £50 million between 2027/28 and 2031/32.

findings.headline: HRA repairs and maintenance overspent by £8.5m due to high-complexity repairs, damp/mould cases, and Awaab's Law statutory obligations expanding further from October 2026
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account repairs outturn was £25.9m against £17.4m budget, a £8.5m overspend. Drivers include high volume of complex repairs, increased damp and mould cases, and Awaab's Law obligations (in force 27 October 2025) expanding to further hazard categories from October 2026. Interest costs also rose £2.0m due to higher borrowing rates. Combined with HRA self-referral to Regulator of Social Housing, the stock faces mounting regulatory and maintenance cost pressure.
findings.matters: HRA now faces mandatory statutory repairs obligations (Awaab's Law) that expand further, driving costs beyond current assumptions. This combines with an ageing housing stock and regulatory scrutiny to create multiple structural pressures on HRA business plan sustainability.
findings.figures: £8.5m repairs overspend (£25.9m actual vs £17.4m budget); interest costs £2.0m over budget; complex repairs and damp/mould cases driving volume; Awaab's Law obligations expanding October 2026
findings.quote: Demand for repairs and maintenance services remained significantly above budgeted levels. A high volume of complex repairs, an increase in damp and mould cases, and the transition to new service contracts placed sustained pressure on the budget, alongside the new statutory obligations introduced by Awaab's Law, which came into force for the social rented sector on 27 October 2025.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £102.3m (31% of budget) with £40m I4B loan facility undrawn and 543 council homes delivered against 820 target (34% below)
findings.detail: The council delivered £209.8m capital against revised budget of £328.9m. Slippage of £102.3m includes £41.9m I4B facility (loan and equity not drawn, expected 2026/27), £23.8m Housing General Fund (only 31 of planned properties acquired), 543 homes completed vs 820 target. The report attributes slippage to 'inherent complexity', late funding announcements, 'constrained contractor market', and procurement law changes. This carries forward commitments and financing costs into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Slippage at 31% of budget raises questions about the realism of future capital plans. The I4B facility not being drawn and housing targets missed 34% suggest either overambitious planning or execution capacity constraints. Carrying commitments forward extends financing costs in a higher interest rate environment.
findings.figures: £102.3m slippage (31% of revised budget); £41.9m I4B undrawn; 543 homes delivered vs 820 target (66%); Housing GF £17.2m underspend from lower property prices than budgeted
findings.quote: The level of slippage across the 2025/26 Capital Programme reflects the inherent complexity of delivering a large investment programme in a challenging operating environment. Ambitious NCIL and SCIL schemes received Cabinet approval later in the financial year, compressing the time available for delivery.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection remains 0.9 percentage points below target at 91.6% despite structured improvement plan, with working-age CTS recipients showing only 78% collection and debt recovery arrears risk flagged
findings.detail: The 2025/26 collection target was 92.5% but actual was 91.6%. Although 0.4pp better than 2024/25, it remains below target. Working-age Council Tax Support recipients achieved only 78% collection with 69% making any payment. The report states low in-year collection 'is a key risk to the Council's financial resilience in the medium term' because debt becomes significantly harder to collect after two years.
findings.matters: Collection below target despite an external review and improvement plan signals persistent underlying collection weakness. The council has explicitly identified continued low collection as a medium-term financial resilience risk, particularly on debt that will be harder to recover after two years.
findings.figures: 91.6% actual vs 92.5% target; 78% collection rate on working-age CTS; only 69% of CTS recipients made payment toward 2025/26 bill; £1.5m Hardship Fund deployed to support payment
findings.quote: Evidence suggests that debt becomes much harder to collect after two years have passed, so the continued low in-year collection of Council Tax is a key risk to the Council's financial resilience in the medium term.

findings.headline: Quarter 4 purchase order review uncovered material untracked expenditure in Strategic Commissioning, exposing forecasting control weaknesses and requiring new governance procedures
findings.detail: Strategic Commissioning recorded £2.9m overspend. In Q4, a detailed Purchase Order review identified significant expenditure not captured in earlier forecasts, 'resulting in a large adjustment to the year-end position.' The report directly states this 'highlighted weaknesses in the end-to-end Purchase Order process, particularly around reconciliation.' Extra care placements were found to now cost as much as residential care despite being intended as cost-effective alternative. New controls are being implemented including formal logging of all spend outside approved contracts.
findings.matters: Untracked expenditure discovered in Q4 indicates control weaknesses in how commitments are monitored and reflected in forecasts. This undermines the reliability of in-year financial reporting and suggests forecast revisions could surprise materially late in the year.
findings.figures: £2.9m overspend; £2.6m in Commissioning and Contracts; material Purchase Orders not captured in forecasts
findings.quote: During Quarter 4, a detailed review of Purchase Orders was undertaken. This exercise identified expenditure that had not been captured in previous forecasts, resulting in a large adjustment to the year-end position. The findings highlighted weaknesses in the end-to-end Purchase Order process, particularly around reconciliation and the timely reflection of commitments within financial forecasts.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit has grown to £20.2m on the back of 10.6% annual increase in Education, Health and Care Plans
findings.detail: DSG recorded £6.6m in-year deficit (worse than £4.8m Q3 forecast). The High Needs Block overspent £8.2m driven by increased top-up funding for special school placements. EHCPs rose from 3,892 to 4,306 (10.6% increase). Cumulative DSG deficit grew from £13.6m (end 2024/25) to £20.2m and cannot be funded from the General Fund without Secretary of State approval under regulations that run until end 2027/28.
findings.matters: DSG deficit is effectively ringfenced and growing, representing an unfunded liability. The annual 10.6% increase in EHCPs signals structural pressure that will continue. This is off-balance-sheet commitments that constrain financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £6.6m in-year deficit (vs £4.8m forecast); £20.2m cumulative deficit (up from £13.6m); EHCPs 4,306 (up 10.6% from 3,892); High Needs Block £8.2m overspend
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25, the cumulative DSG deficit stood at £13.6m, reflecting the sustained increases in demand for High Needs provision and ongoing pressures on top-up funding. Following 2025/26 in year deficit of £6.6m, the overall cumulative DSG deficit has now increased to £20.2m.

findings.headline: Homelessness applications surged 40% year-on-year to 8,795, with 1,428 households in nightly-paid temporary accommodation and no funded structural solution identified
findings.detail: Housing Needs and Support recorded £11.7m overspend, the largest pressure in the General Fund. Applications rose from 6,281 in March 2025 to 8,795 by year end, averaging 169 per week. Nightly-paid accommodation increased from 1,182 households in April 2025 to 1,428 by April 2026. The overspend grew £7.2m between Q3 and Q4 alone. The Cabinet Member's foreword explicitly states the council 'cannot by itself reverse demographic change, reshape the national care market or correct the wider failure of London's housing market.'
findings.matters: This is the council's most urgent and deteriorating problem. A 40% year-on-year rise in applications is unsustainable, the council has no policy levers to address root causes, and costs are spiralling. This poses a material risk to medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £11.7m overspend; 8,795 total applications by year end; 1,428 households in nightly-paid accommodation; 40% increase vs March 2025; 169 new applications per week; Q4 movement alone £7.2m
findings.quote: By the end of 2025/26, Brent had received a total of 8,795 homelessness support applications, comprising 5,309 single individuals and 3,486 families. This equates to an average of approximately 169 new applications per week, highlighting the sustained and intense demand for housing services. This reflects a 40% increase compared with March 2025, when total applications stood at 6,281

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £7.0m with £1.3m of planned savings unachieved, driven by placement costs rising 26% and care complexity exceeding budget assumptions
findings.detail: The directorate delivered only £3.5m of its £4.8m savings target. Cost pressures exceeded all assumptions: homecare hours up 3.4%, residential dementia placements up 40.1%, nursing dementia up 10.9%, new placement costs rising over 26%. Learning Disability supported living packages increased 5.6% with average weekly costs up 9.5%. The council explicitly states these cost increases exceed the growth assumptions built into the budget.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the council's largest controllable spend but cost drivers are outpacing provision of funding. Unachieved savings signal the budget is not deliverable in a higher-cost market. A lender needs visibility of whether this pattern will continue.
findings.figures: £7.0m overspend; £1.3m unachieved savings from £4.8m target; residential dementia +40.1%; nursing dementia +10.9%; new placement costs +26%; Learning Disability supported living packages +5.6%
findings.quote: The scale of these cost increases, which exceed the growth assumptions built into the 2025/26 budget, has created significant challenges in delivering planned savings. Of the £4.8m savings required for the year, £1.3m remain unachieved.

findings.headline: Integrated Care Board funding disputes creating unfunded cost exposure for complex care packages
findings.detail: There is a significant financial risk from disputes and delays in agreeing cost-sharing arrangements with the Integrated Care Board (ICB) for complex care packages. In 2025/26, income contributions from the ICB should have totalled £1.3m, but delays in agreement continued to impact financial planning. The council carries the cost exposure until agreements are reached, which can take many months.
findings.matters: Relying on partner contributions that are consistently delayed creates cash-flow risk and forces the council to fund services ahead of receiving the income. This is an inter-agency governance issue that erodes financial predictability.
findings.figures: ICB contributions expected £1.3m in 2025/26 but subject to ongoing delays
findings.quote: There remains a significant financial risk arising from disputes and delays in agreeing cost-sharing arrangements with the Integrated Care Board (ICB) for complex care packages. In a number of cases, engagement with the ICB has not resulted in timely resolution, leading to prolonged uncertainty over funding contributions and increasing pressure on the Council's budgets. For 2025/26, income contributions from the ICB totalled £1.3m; however, delays in agreement continue to impact financial planning and expose the Council to potential unfunded costs.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's placement costs remain volatile with potential for significant overspends if demand moves adversely
findings.detail: Adult Social Care forecasts a breakeven position, but section 4.5 notes a potential risk of £3.5m overspend if supported living and residential care demand continues at current elevated levels (new packages are 14-16% more expensive than those ending). Children's placements are forecast to breakeven but section 4.24 shows the outturn could range from £1.4m underspend to £3.2m overspend depending on whether residential placements end the year at 44 or 58 (an allowance of 53 is built into the forecast). These are inherently unpredictable demand-led budgets.
findings.matters: Both Adult and Children's social care are showing early-year demand pressures that could materialize as overspends within months. The council has only limited levers to contain these costs (e.g., reviewing high-cost packages, opening in-house provision). If both overspend, the total exposure could easily exceed £5m.
findings.figures: Potential £3.5m Adult Social Care overspend if demand continues; Children's placements range from £1.4m underspend to £3.2m overspend; new care packages running 14-16% more expensive than those ending
findings.quote: In comparison to the 2026/27 modelling for Adults Placements that informed budget setting, at Q1 the trend indicates that homecare demand has been reduced but the demand for supported living and residential care have increased as with clients with more complex needs being placed, indicating a potential risk of £3.5m overspend if this is not mitigated.

findings.headline: Some directorate savings targets at risk; lane rental scheme and padel courts initiatives delayed
findings.detail: Children, Young People & Community Development reports £0.4m of allocated savings at risk, primarily relating to digital transformation and commissioning activity. Neighbourhoods & Regeneration's Lane Rental scheme was expected to come operational in Autumn 2026 but approval transfer from DfT to London Mayor has delayed it; unlikely to generate income in 2026/27. Padel Courts asset utilisation saving has not yet confirmed its delivery model. If these savings cannot be delivered, it creates in-year overspends and requires finding alternative savings elsewhere.
findings.matters: Early-year savings shortfalls signal that the £10.4m total savings package may not be fully deliverable. If multiple departmental savings fail to materialize, the council will lack the flexibility to contain the £9.5m General Fund overspend.
findings.figures: £0.4m of CYP savings at risk; Lane Rental income generation now at zero for 2026/27; Padel Courts delivery model not yet confirmed
findings.quote: £0.4m of the directorate's allocated savings is currently assessed to be at risk, primarily relating to savings linked to digital transformation and commissioning and procurement activity. There is also Lane Rental scheme delays: It was expected the Lane Rental scheme would come into operation in Autumn 2026 and immediately generate income for the Council. There are delays to this scheme whilst its approval transfers from DfT to the London Mayor, and it is now unlikely to be operational and generate any income in 2026/27.

findings.headline: HRA is balanced but faces material building-safety compliance costs following Regulator's C3 judgement
findings.detail: The HRA is reporting a breakeven position for 2026/27, but section 7.9 references a "C3 judgement" from the Regulator requiring building-safety compliance work. Remediation and recovery costs are still being quantified, with comparable authorities incurring around £2.3m in similar circumstances. There is also a risk to grant funding for housing development while the council operates under regulatory scrutiny until full compliance is demonstrated.
findings.matters: A regulator-mandated remediation programme on top of normal HRA cost pressures (inflation, Awaab's Law compliance, repairs demand) could absorb reserves or require additional borrowing. The C3 judgement indicates prior governance weaknesses in asset management.
findings.figures: Comparable authorities incurred around £2.3m in building-safety remediation costs in similar circumstances; exact costs for Brent still being quantified
findings.quote: The Council has since been delivering a Housing and Asset Management Service Improvement Plan, with regular engagement with the Regulator, and reports that that good progress is being made, with stock-condition survey coverage now above 70% of homes with the target of 100% planned on being achieved this year. The programme nonetheless remains a significant risk and financial pressure on the HRA: remediation and recovery costs are still being quantified, with comparable authorities reportedly incurring around £2.3m in similar circumstances.

findings.headline: Supported Exempt Accommodation overspend of £2.1m in 2025/26 represents unbudgeted cost pressure outside normal temporary accommodation frameworks
findings.detail: Supported Exempt Accommodation providers are not bound by Local Housing Allowance caps and charge higher rents once they claim support services are provided. Housing Benefit subsidy levels then follow Rent Officer determinations. An overspend of £2.1m occurred in 2025/26 (historically these were managed within corporate central budgets), and this area remains "carefully monitored" as a budgetary risk for 2026/27. The council has established a dedicated working group but the issue reflects a national problem with unclear regulation.
findings.matters: This is an uncontrolled cost driver within the homelessness system that sits outside normal budget frameworks. The £2.1m 2025/26 overspend suggests the cost could repeat or grow in 2026/27, and there is no clear mitigation other than regulatory reform at national level.
findings.figures: £2.1m overspend in Supported Exempt Accommodation in 2025/26
findings.quote: an overspend of £2.1m occurred in 2025/26 and this area of spend being carefully monitored. A dedicated working group has been established within the Council with the objective to carefully assess individuals' support care needs and verify that providers are delivering the appropriate level of care.

findings.headline: Building Control income has structurally declined and is unlikely to recover under new Building Safety regulatory regime
findings.detail: Since the Building Safety Act introduced in October 2023, Higher Risk Building applications must go to the Building Safety Regulator on a cost-recovery basis. This has caused a sustained and structural reduction in council income from Building Control work. The council faces a legal requirement under CIPFA guidance to balance income with eligible costs, meaning income targets need to be reset lower. Workforce retention is also challenging due to sector-wide shortage of qualified surveyors.
findings.matters: Building Control income underpins part of the council's income-generating capacity. A structural decline in an income stream that cannot be reversed under the new regulatory regime creates a permanent reduction in capacity to self-fund services, requiring either service reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Building Control income targets were set when major project income was significantly higher; income has not recovered post-Building Safety Act implementation; vacancies in surveyor roles remain unfilled
findings.quote: Since the introduction of the Building Safety Act (BSA) in October 2023, Higher Risk Building applications must be made to the Building Safety Regulator and charged on a cost recovery basis. This change, alongside reduced major development activity, has resulted in a sustained and structural reduction in income that is unlikely to reverse under the new regulatory regime.

findings.headline: Economic environment deteriorated since February budget-setting with inflation and interest rates likely to remain elevated
findings.detail: CPI inflation is at 2.8% (March: 3.0%), with the Bank of England now expecting it to remain higher for longer than the 2.5% average assumed in February. Interest rates remain at 3.75% following a December cut, with further cuts now unlikely if inflation stays elevated. Both factors were not anticipated when the budget was set and create a material risk to both council service delivery costs (pay, procurement inflation) and capital financing costs.
findings.matters: The £10.4m savings package that was sufficient to balance the budget in February is now under pressure from inflation, and borrowing costs for the capital programme will be higher than assumed. This creates an early-warning signal that in-year savings shortfalls are likely.
findings.figures: CPI at 2.8% (April 2026) vs 2.5% budget assumption; interest rates at 3.75% vs expected gradual fall to 3.25%; £10.4m of agreed savings may not be sufficient to balance budget given inflation pressures
findings.quote: CPI inflation increased to just over 3% in March before easing slightly to 2.8% in April. The Bank of England now expects inflation to remain higher for the rest of 2026 than previously forecast, compared with the February assumption of an average rate of 2.5%. Higher inflation increases the cost of delivering council services and creates a risk of overspending in 2026/27 compared with the budget agreed earlier in the year.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit forecast to reach £38.4m by year-end with no clear funding solution
findings.detail: The DSG is forecasting an in-year overspend of £18.2m in 2026/27, on top of a brought-forward deficit of £20.2m. The High Needs Block (SEND provision) alone is overspent by £19.6m. The core driver is a 10.6% increase in children with EHCPs (3,892 to 4,306 between March 2025-2026) and a 12.6% increase in placements in independent schools due to insufficient in-borough capacity. The Government has offered to fund 90% of accumulated deficits up to March 2026, but this is conditional on delivering a local SEND Reform Plan and leaves future year deficits unresolved.
findings.matters: Growing SEND demand is driving a statutory deficit that will transfer to the General Fund from April 2028 when the Government's statutory override expires. Without material reduction in SEND demand or major funding reform, this creates an unknown but material liability for the General Fund within 3 years.
findings.figures: £18.2m in-year overspend forecast; cumulative deficit rising to £38.4m by year-end; 10.6% increase in EHCPs (3,892 to 4,306); 12.6% increase in independent school placements; High Needs Block £19.6m overspend
findings.quote: The High Needs Block budget is forecast to face a funding deficit of £19.6m in 2026/27. This reflects significant and sustained budget pressures arising from a 10.6% increase in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) as of March 2026, alongside a 12.6% increase in the number of Brent children placed in independent schools over the same period due to insufficient provision within the borough. No additional growth funding has been provided in 2026/27 to address this rising demand or inflationary cost pressures.

findings.headline: General Fund facing £9.5m overspend entirely from homelessness emergency accommodation costs
findings.detail: The entire overspend is concentrated in Housing Needs and Support. In April 2026 there were 1,428 households in nightly paid accommodation, up from 1,182 a year earlier (a 9% increase since December 2025). At £326 per week per household on average, even small demand movements create significant cost swings. The service already began the year with a structural £3.7m overspend built into the forecast.
findings.matters: If a £9.5m Q1 overspend is not arrested, it will require drawing unallocated reserves before year-end, weakening the council's financial resilience going into 2027/28 when further demand pressures are expected.
findings.figures: £9.5m overspend forecast; 1,428 households in nightly paid accommodation (April 2026) vs 1,182 (April 2025); £326 average per week per household; £3.7m structural deficit at year start
findings.quote: The Housing Needs and Support budget overspent by £11.7m in 2025/26 due to an extremely high level of demand for this service and a lack of affordable Private Rented Sector (PRS) offers. In 2026/27, £8m of growth was built into the base budget, to deal with continuous pressures and demand. Accordingly, this places the 2026/27 budget in a £3.7m overspend position at the outset.

findings.headline: Large subsidiary loan portfolio of £287.5m depends on rental income to cover £6.0m annual debt service costs
findings.detail: The council holds £287.5m in service investments: £179.2m loaned to i4B Holdings (PRS housing company for homeless prevention) and £33.4m to First Wave Housing (216 rental properties). Interest income from these loans was £6.0m, which the report states 'covers the borrowing cost of investing in housing through wholly owned subsidiaries'. The council's ability to service its own debt therefore depends on these subsidiaries maintaining rental income.
findings.matters: A sharp decline in rental income (housing market downturn, void rates, welfare policy changes) would leave the council unable to recover its debt service costs and exposed to uncompensated borrowing.
findings.figures: Total service investments £287.5m; i4B loans £179.2m; First Wave loans £33.4m; interest income £6.0m
findings.quote: These investments generated £6.0m of income for the Council in 2025/26 (£6.0m in 2024/25). This investment income covers the borrowing cost of investing in housing through wholly owned subsidiaries.

findings.headline: Two LOBO loans repaid when lenders forced rate increases to 6.41% and 6.24%, plus £9.5m more due for review in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council held £59.5m in LOBO loans (lender option to force rate increase). Two loans totalling £20m were repaid in 2025/26 after lenders exercised options: one increasing from 4.1% to 6.41%, another from 5.2% to 6.24%. The council chose to repay and refinance through PWLB rather than accept the new rates. A further £9.5m LOBO loan has a rate review due in 2026/27, creating similar refinancing risk.
findings.matters: LOBO loans expose the council to forced refinancing at the worst times (when lenders see rising rates as opportunity). The council cannot control these events and has limited negotiating power once the option is exercised.
findings.figures: LOBO loans repaid 2025/26: £10.0m at 4.1% (new rate 6.41%), £10.0m at 5.2% (new rate 6.24%); remaining LOBO £39.5m; further LOBO £9.5m due for review 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council repaid two LOBO loans in 2025/26 after the lender exercised their option. As a result, the Council's borrowing requirement increased, with the additional financing being met through borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) during the year within our overall borrowing need.

findings.headline: New borrowing locked in at 5%+ rates while portfolio averages 3.9%, increasing future debt service burden
findings.detail: The council's average borrowing rate increased from 3.85% to 3.90%, despite falling Bank Rate and gilt yields during the year. New PWLB borrowing (£230m raised) was at 5%+ rates (10-year certainty rate 5.72% at year-end), which exceeds the existing portfolio average. The report explicitly notes that while interest rates fell, available PWLB rates remained higher than the council's existing debt portfolio average, so new lending added debt at above-average cost.
findings.matters: Raising £230m+ of new debt at rates above the portfolio average locks in higher future debt service costs and eliminates the benefit of any future interest rate cuts.
findings.figures: Average rate 3.85% → 3.90%; PWLB 10-year rate 5.4% → 5.7%; new PWLB borrowing £230.0m at EIP basis
findings.quote: Whilst interest rates fell during the year, the rates available for new PWLB borrowing remained higher than the average rate payable across the Council's existing debt portfolio. Consequently, the addition of new borrowing increased the overall weighted average cost of debt, albeit only marginally.

findings.headline: Working capital increase of £70m is non-cash: driven by debtors (money owed to council) rather than cash received
findings.detail: Working capital rose £69.6m (89.6 → 159.2), primarily from a £70m increase in debtors. However, the council explicitly states this increase in debtors 'did not translate into higher cash available for investment' because the timing of receipt remains uncertain. Cash balances continued to be used to fund the capital programme despite the working capital improvement, showing the council has not actually received the money it is now owed.
findings.matters: If debtor collection slows or defaults increase (common in economic downturns), the council faces cash pressure despite appearing to have improved working capital. The position is illiquid, not liquid.
findings.figures: Working capital increase £69.6m; of which debtors increase £70m; cash investments fell £3.5m despite this improvement
findings.quote: Although the Council's working capital increased during 2025/26, this was primarily driven by higher year-end debtor balances rather than additional cash resources. As a result, the increase in working capital did not translate into higher cash available for investment, with cash balances continuing to be utilised to support the capital programme and debt repayments.

findings.headline: Net borrowing position deteriorated by £177.6m to £1,030.3m as capital programme accelerated depletion of cash reserves
findings.detail: Net debt (external borrowing less investments) increased from £852.7m to £1,030.3m. External borrowing rose £174.1m to £1,074.1m while cash investments fell £3.5m to £43.8m. Internal borrowing (use of reserves to fund capital) fell from £453.8m to £338.2m—a reduction of £115.6m in a single year—showing the council is burning through financial buffers rapidly.
findings.matters: A deteriorating net debt position with shrinking cash reserves indicates the council has limited financial flexibility to absorb revenue shocks or capital overruns, and may be forced into expensive borrowing if reserves collapse.
findings.figures: Net borrowing £852.7m → £1,030.3m; internal borrowing £453.8m → £338.2m; external debt £900.0m → £1,074.1m

findings.headline: The council is monitoring 14 strategic risks, of which 10 remained above their target risk scores throughout 2025-26, indicating an elevated and dynamic risk environment
findings.detail: The council formally monitors 14 strategic risks at corporate level. Ten of these remained above their target risk scores throughout the year, though the council states each had active mitigation plans in place. A new strategic risk relating to AI governance was introduced during the year, reflecting emerging risks.
findings.matters: Ten of fourteen strategic risks above target (71%) indicates the council operates in an elevated risk environment and considers itself exposed to multiple material risks simultaneously. This provides contextual background on the level of organisational stress beyond specific operational issues.
findings.figures: 14 strategic risks monitored; 10 above target risk scores; 1 new AI governance risk added during year
findings.quote: While ten of these remained above their target risk scores, each had a clear and active mitigation plan in place, and the Council demonstrated continued maturity in its approach by refining controls and adapting risk responses where necessary.

findings.headline: A January-March 2025 Procurement Peer Review identified significant weaknesses in governance, capability and compliance; Internal Audit reinforced findings of inconsistent controls and limited oversight in contract management
findings.detail: The peer review was commissioned due to the Procurement Act 2025 implementation, external audit findings and the transformation programme. Internal Audit work in 2025-26 identified ongoing issues including inconsistent controls, limited oversight, and gaps in performance monitoring and value for money. The council has established a Procurement Improvement Programme and is segmenting 70+ contracts by risk tier.
findings.matters: Procurement control weaknesses directly impact value for money, which is a statutory duty. They also indicate how the council is managing its largest commercial obligations and contract performance monitoring.
findings.figures: 70+ contracts being segmented into tiers for oversight; 19 contract managers to receive practitioner training
findings.quote: Internal Audit work in 2025–26 reinforced these findings, identifying ongoing issues including inconsistent controls, limited oversight, and gaps in performance monitoring and value for money.

findings.headline: Internal Audit provided only qualified 'reasonable assurance' over governance arrangements, with significant improvement areas identified in four major domains: assets, housing compliance, procurement and cross-council control integration
findings.detail: The annual audit opinion was qualified rather than clean. Key improvement areas explicitly identified were: assets and valuations (material control weaknesses), housing compliance (regulatory judgment and data integrity issues), procurement (peer review and control findings), and cross-council ownership/control integration (systemic silo working). These represent the Council's own assessment of significant governance gaps.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion is a material indicator of governance stress. Multiple concurrent areas requiring significant improvement suggests the control environment is under pressure across the organisation, not isolated to one area.
findings.figures: 4 key improvement areas identified; Deputy Director of Organisational Assurance opinion based on audit work in 2025-26
findings.quote: It is the opinion of the Deputy Director of Organisational Assurance and Resilience that, considering all available evidence from audit work undertaken in 2025-26, there is reasonable assurance over the adequacy and effectiveness of the Council's overall framework of governance, risk management and control during the financial year.

findings.headline: Internal Audit identified a recurring pattern of fragmented control ownership and silo working where controls fail at service interfaces, affecting assets, housing compliance, contract management and other areas
findings.detail: Multiple 2025-26 audits identified that while controls often operate effectively within individual teams, weaknesses systematically arise at service boundaries where ownership is shared or unclear. This pattern was observed across multiple reviews including assets, housing compliance, contract management and other control areas.
findings.matters: A fragmented control environment increases the risk that system weaknesses will not be detected or remediated, particularly for enterprise-wide or cross-functional risks. This pattern suggests underlying governance architecture issues that could affect other areas not yet audited.
findings.figures: Pattern identified across multiple 2025-26 audit reviews
findings.quote: Across multiple 2025–26 audits, Internal Audit identified a recurring issue of fragmented ownership and silo working where controls and risks span services. While controls often operate well within teams, weaknesses arise at service interfaces.

findings.headline: The council has identified an anticipated budget gap extending to 2028 and is dependent on delivering £10m of agreed savings in 2026/27 to balance the budget
findings.detail: The council faces sustained demand-led pressures, particularly in temporary accommodation and social care. The Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a multi-year budget gap to 2028 and relies on delivery of transformation savings through the Embrace Change Portfolio for financial resilience rather than one-off measures. External audit commentary recognised significant financial pressures in these demand-led services.
findings.matters: A multi-year budget gap indicates structural financial challenges rather than one-off pressures. Dependency on transformation savings delivery means failure to deliver agreed reductions would open a financing gap, requiring either additional savings, service reductions, or external funding.
findings.figures: £10m of savings agreed for 2026/27; anticipated budget gap identified to 2028
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies an anticipated budget gap up to 2028 and sets out the work underway to address this through enhanced financial planning, strengthened transformation activity and delivery of savings through the Embrace Change Portfolio.

findings.headline: Internal Audit identified significant control weaknesses in the council's 15,000+ property asset portfolio, causing a 3-week delay in 2024/25 accounts preparation and continued external audit delays
findings.detail: The Fixed Asset Register (FAR) and Property Asset Register (PAR) were not properly governed, reconciled or maintained. The PAR was manual, incomplete and not CIPFA compliant. Testing found data gaps, missing supporting evidence, inconsistent reference numbers and reconciliation problems across systems. This contributed to prior-year audit delays and required auditors to repeat procedures. The council is establishing cross-council working groups to address this but further work is continuing.
findings.matters: Asset accounting controls are fundamental to the reliability of financial statements and the council's balance sheet. Control weaknesses in property valuations and fixed asset registers directly impact the accuracy of reported asset values which underpin any asset-backed borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Over 15,000 assets in portfolio; 3-week delay in 2024/25 accounts preparation; external audit also noted PPE balance issues significantly affected audit timing
findings.quote: During 2025–26, Internal Audit identified significant weaknesses in the governance and control environment supporting the Council's two key registers: the Finance-led Fixed Asset Register (FAR) and the Property-led Property Asset Register (PAR).

findings.headline: Brent received a C3 regulatory judgment from the Regulator of Social Housing in May 2025 due to material safety compliance failures across 8,800 council homes
findings.detail: The regulatory judgment related to the Safety and Quality Standard and was triggered by self-assessment findings in March 2025 which identified that Fire Risk Assessment actions had been recorded as complete without sufficient evidence, with similar issues in water safety and asbestos compliance. Survey records were missing for more than half of the council's housing stock. The council has commissioned specialist external advisers and established strengthened governance through the Housing and Tenant Satisfaction Improvement Programme.
findings.matters: A C3 judgment from the housing regulator signals control failures in a core council function affecting resident safety. The scale of the issue—8,800 homes with incomplete safety records—is material to understanding the council's operating environment and remediation obligations.
findings.figures: 8,800 council homes; more than half of stock missing survey data; council committed to 35% survey coverage in current year, full coverage by March 2028
findings.quote: In March 2025, a self-assessment of data held within the True Compliance system highlighted concerns about the management of key building safety areas. In particular, actions arising from Fire Risk Assessments had been recorded as complete without sufficient evidence, and similar issues were identified in water safety and asbestos compliance processes.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: Council identified 3 significant weaknesses in arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in use of resources
findings.detail: Under the National Audit Office Code of Audit Practice, auditors identified 3 significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. These findings are reported in detail in the separate Auditor's Annual Report presented to the September 2025 Audit & Standards Committee.
findings.matters: Significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements indicate broader governance and management issues that could affect the council's operational efficiency and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 3 significant weaknesses identified
findings.quote: We identified 3 significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: Material financial instruments errors: £30.7m payables and £26.4m debtors misclassification requiring prior period adjustment
findings.detail: Auditors identified material errors in management's assessment of short-term debtors and creditors against IFRS 9 classification criteria. Management completed a full re-assessment confirming material errors existed in both current and prior year figures. Revised notes confirmed: Note 24 Payables - £30.7m reduction in financial liabilities; Note 24 Debtors - £26.4m reduction in financial assets, requiring prior period adjustment and restatement of prior year comparatives.
findings.matters: Material errors of this magnitude in financial instrument classification indicate systematic weaknesses in accounting processes and suggest the council's underlying financial position reporting may be materially unreliable.
findings.figures: £30.7m payables adjustment; £26.4m debtors adjustment
findings.quote: Material errors existed in both the current and prior year figures for the debtor and creditor balances reported in these notes. Management agreed that a PPA was required to restate the prior year comparators.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: Oracle Fusion system has excessive administrative permissions granted to business users without clear justification, creating management override risk
findings.detail: IT audit identified a significant deficiency in security management of the main ledger system, with excessive system administrative permissions granted to business users without clear justification. This was rated Red for security management. The control deficiency was factored into the journal testing strategy to address the inherent risk of management override of controls.
findings.matters: Excessive system permissions without proper justification create elevated risk of unauthorized or fraudulent transactions being recorded in the financial statements without detection.
findings.figures: Oracle Fusion security management rated Red
findings.quote: There is a risk arising from excessive system administrative permissions granted to business users without clear justification.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 implementation discovered £5.7m error in lease liability calculations and £7m double-counted asset
findings.detail: IFRS 16 implementation resulted in first-time recognition of right-of-use (ROU) assets of £19.8m. However, testing identified a £5.7m error caused by incorrect calculation of lease liability calculations and a lease asset (£7m) double counted in both lessees and lessors. The entire leases disclosure was subsequently rewritten when management identified a significant volume of errors in the underlying data.
findings.matters: Material errors in the first-year implementation of a new accounting standard indicate implementation challenges and systemic data quality problems affecting the reliability of asset valuations.
findings.figures: £19.8m ROU assets; £5.7m calculation error; £7m double-counted; £28.8m PFI assets added
findings.quote: This figure was updated following our testing, which identified a £5.7m error caused by incorrect calculation of the lease liability calculations and a lease (£7m) double counted in both lessees and lessors.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: £3.7m capital expenditure error: 2024-25 costs incorrectly recorded in 2025-26 due to lack of management review
findings.detail: An error of £3.7m was identified where expenditure relating to the 2024-25 financial year was incorrectly recorded in 2025-26, resulting in an understatement of 2024-25 expenditure. Both this error and a £1.2m creditors error arose because of a lack of management review of capital accruals during the year. Management subsequently agreed to strengthen the review process of capital accruals.
findings.matters: Material errors in capital expenditure recognition indicate weak period-end financial controls and could mask true spending positions, affecting creditors' assessment of the council's financial management capability.
findings.figures: £3.7m error in capital expenditure; £1.2m creditors error identified in extended testing
findings.quote: An error of £3.7m was identified where expenditure relating to the 2024–25 financial year was incorrectly recorded in 2025–26, resulting in an understatement of 2024–25 expenditure. Both errors arose because of a lack of management review of capital accruals during the year.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: Draft financial statements delayed by one month, missing statutory publication deadline
findings.detail: The draft 2024-25 financial statements were not delivered by the agreed date of 18 July 2025 and were delayed until 18 August 2025, missing the 30 June 2025 statutory publication deadline. The main reason for delay continues to be PPE valuation problems including receipt of incorrect valuation reports, duplicate property valuations, difficulties reconciling the fixed asset register with valuation reports, and slow responses from the valuer.
findings.matters: Missing the statutory audit deadline indicates governance and financial reporting timeliness issues affecting stakeholder confidence and triggering regulatory scrutiny under the Local Audit and Accountability Act.
findings.figures: Delayed from 18 July to 18 August 2025 (one month); statutory deadline 30 June 2025
findings.quote: The draft 2024-25 financial statements was not delivered by the agreed date of 18 July 2025, and delayed until 18 August 2025, missing the 30 June 2025 statutory publication deadline.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: HRA garage valuations discovered to be £6.5m understated, material valuation error in asset register
findings.detail: Management shared HRA garage valuations carried out separately by an independent valuer revealing significant discrepancy: the new valuation of the garages is £11.3m, compared to £4.8m in the FAR and draft accounts, resulting in a £6.5m error. Management confirmed ownership of 706 garages and 2 cages which were tested with no issues identified after valuation.
findings.matters: Material valuation errors of this magnitude indicate ongoing problems in the council's property valuation processes and suggest the £972m property portfolio may contain other undetected valuation errors.
findings.figures: £6.5m error (£11.3m actual vs £4.8m recorded); 706 garages and 2 cages
findings.quote: The new valuation of the garages is £11.3m, compared to £4.8m in the FAR/draft accounts, resulting in a £6.5m error.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: Segregation of duties control failure: 9 of 20 journals tested (45%) posted by individuals outside their remit
findings.detail: Testing identified that 9 out of 20 journals tested were posted by an individual outside of their remit. Middle management who approved these journals in the system had prepared the journals and instructed the individual to post them, before subsequently approving them in the system. While all cases had an additional layer of approval outside the system, this creates a significant segregation of duties issue raising concerns about potential management override.
findings.matters: Weak segregation of duties in journal posting increases the risk that unauthorized, erroneous, or fraudulent transactions could be recorded in the financial statements without adequate independent review.
findings.figures: 9 out of 20 journals (45%)
findings.quote: 9 out of 20 journals tested were found to be posted by an individual outside of their remit. Furthermore, middle management who approved these journals in the system had prepared the journals and instructed the individual to post them, before subsequently approving them in the system.

findings.paper_title: Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for the London Borough of Brent 2024-25
findings.headline: £19m of assets written off and £79m misclassified in property, plant and equipment requiring major prior period adjustment
findings.detail: During 2024-25 management undertook a cleansing exercise of the fixed asset register (FAR) which identified approximately £19m of assets that could not be supported and were written off or disposed of, and around £79m of assets that were misclassified between PPE categories. Testing identified a material issue with the approach and preparation of management's PPA calculation, with further material reclassifications still required in both current and prior years.
findings.matters: Suggests systematic data quality failures in the council's £972m property portfolio, undermining confidence in asset valuations and the reliability of financial records.
findings.figures: £19m written off/disposed; £79m misclassified; £972m total PPE net book value
findings.quote: Approximately £19m of assets could not be supported and were written off or disposed of from the FAR. Around £79m of assets were misclassified between PPE categories.

findings.headline: Statutory override allowing DSG deficit separation from general revenue budget ends 2028, creating unsustainable position without government support continuation
findings.detail: The statutory override that allows local authorities to hold DSG deficits separately from general revenue balances has been extended to 2028. Once the override ends, any remaining DSG deficit would need to be managed within the general revenue budget, potentially impacting overall council solvency. Modelling shows a potential £46m cumulative deficit by March 2028 without government support. While government has confirmed future SEND costs will be 'managed within the overall government Departmental Expenditure Limits (DEL), meaning local authorities will not be expected to fund future SEND costs from general funds once the statutory override ends in 2028', this commitment requires government follow-through on reform promises.
findings.matters: The 2028 cliff-edge represents a critical solvency risk if: (1) government does not deliver on its DEL commitment, (2) EHCP demand continues growing without matching funding, or (3) the council cannot deliver the reforms necessary to secure ongoing grant support. This creates a dependency on government delivery of its SEND reform agenda.
findings.figures: Override ends 2028; potential £46m cumulative deficit by March 2028 without grant support; override currently extended to 2028 'pending wider reform'
findings.quote: The statutory override that allows local authorities to hold deficit balances against their DSG budgets, separating this from their general revenue budgets, has been extended to 2028 under the current government, pending wider reform of the system. Not taking into account any further grant funding from central government to support the cumulative deficit, the modelling of the current DSG Deficit Management Plan shows the cumulative deficit could increase to £29m by March 2027 and £46m by the end of March 2028 when the statutory override is planned to end.

findings.headline: Capital programme Phase 2 will deliver 212 new places but leaves majority of identified need unmet, with completion phased to 2030
findings.detail: Phase 1 of the capital programme (approved January 2022) has delivered 298 additional places, with 84 more expected by January 2030. Phase 2 (approved January 2026) will add 212 new places focused on special school provision. The programme is projected to achieve £4.3m cost avoidance over its duration (including £2.6m in 2026/27) plus £1.3m transport cost savings, based on average £21k per-place cost avoidance between in-borough and independent provision. However, this addresses only 212 of the 362-place shortfall, and completion is phased to 2030, meaning the gap will persist for several years.
findings.matters: While the capital programme demonstrates management action and provides meaningful cost avoidance, it is insufficient in scale and timing to resolve the underlying capacity problem that drives high-cost independent placements. Cost avoidance is modest relative to the £18.4m deficit.
findings.figures: Phase 1: 298 places delivered, 84 more by Jan 2030; Phase 2: 212 new places; £4.3m cost avoidance over programme duration; £2.6m in 2026/27; £1.3m transport savings; average £21k per-place cost avoidance; completion phased to 2030
findings.quote: The Phase 2 capital programme will deliver an additional 212 places for children with SEND in Brent focused on special school places. Based on the proposed completion dates, the programme could achieve potential cost avoidance of £4.3m over its duration, including £2.6m in 2026/27. This is based on creating 212 new places, with an average cost avoidance of £21k per place, representing the difference between placing a Brent child in an independent special school versus an in-borough special school.

findings.headline: Shortfall of 362 special school places (212 primary, 150 secondary) against identified need forces reliance on expensive independent sector at £51.4k per place per annum
findings.detail: Analysis shows Brent needs 1,221 special school places total (634 primary, 587 secondary) to accommodate all eligible EHCP children. The council currently has only 977 places available (480 primary, 497 secondary), leaving a shortfall of 212 primary and 150 secondary places. This capacity gap forces use of independent non-maintained special schools (INMSS), out-of-borough placements, and home tuition. INMSS spending has reached £12.6m in 2025/26 for 245 places at an average cost of £51.4k per place per annum, an increase of £1m (8.5%) compared to 2024/25.
findings.matters: The capacity shortfall is fundamental to the deficit problem—it forces high-cost alternative placements outside the council's control. INMSS costs are significantly higher than in-borough provision and rising faster than the deficit reduction plan assumes.
findings.figures: 1,221 places needed vs 977 available; 212 primary shortfall + 150 secondary shortfall = 362 total; INMSS spend £12.6m for 245 places; £51.4k per place per annum; £1m increase (8.5% growth) from 2024/25
findings.quote: Brent would require a total of 1,221 places (634 primary and 587 secondary)... Brent currently has 480 places in primary age special school classes and 497 places in secondary age special school places. Brent has a current shortfall of 212 primary places in special and 150 secondary places in special. Brent is currently forecasting spend of £12.6m on INMSS provision for the 2025/26 financial year for 245 places (£51.4k/place/annum), an increase of £1m (and 8.5%) as compared with send on INMSS in the 2024/25.

findings.headline: 90% government grant funding conditional on approved SEND Reform Plan, with future support 'not unlimited' and tied to national policy changes
findings.detail: Government has confirmed grant funding covering 90% of accumulated SEND deficits up to March 2026, but this is explicitly 'subject to an agreed local SEND Reform Plan'. Future support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be 'similarly proportionate' but 'not unlimited'. Critically, all government support is conditional on assurance that the council is 'taking steps to deliver a reformed, inclusive SEND system, aligned with the wider national reforms expected to be confirmed in the forthcoming Schools White Paper' (expected Spring 2026), creating uncertainty about the final shape of funding arrangements.
findings.matters: Lenders face uncertainty about the sustainability of government grant support beyond March 2026. Support is not assured—it depends on successful completion of reform plans and compliance with national policy changes that have not yet been defined, creating a contingent funding model.
findings.figures: 90% of accumulated deficit covered to end March 2026; future support 'not unlimited'; support conditional on approved SEND Reform Plan
findings.quote: The government has confirmed that grant funding will be allocated to cover 90% of local authorities' accumulated SEND deficits up to the end of March 2026, subject to an agreed local SEND Reform Plan. The government has confirmed that local authorities can expect a similarly proportionate approach to the financial support offered to cover deficits up until the end of March 2026 for the deficits that arise in 2026/27 and 2027/28, though this will not be unlimited.

findings.headline: EHCP demand growing at 8-10% annually while DSG High Needs Block funding grows only 3-6.7%, creating structural mismatch
findings.detail: The number of EHCPs in Brent has increased 8% from January 2024 to January 2025, with a long-term trend of 10% annual growth in line with national averages. In contrast, DSG HNB allocation has only increased 3% in 2024/25, 6% in 2025/26, and 4.7% in 2026/27. This fundamental mismatch between demand and funding is identified as the main cost driver and is described as a long-standing problem contributing to sustained financial pressures.
findings.matters: This structural problem shows no sign of resolution through local action alone, meaning the deficit will continue to grow year on year even with capital investment and operational efficiency drives, creating ongoing pressure on the council's finances.
findings.figures: EHCP growth 8% Jan 2024 to Jan 2025; 10% historical trend; DSG HNB growth 3% (2024/25), 6% (2025/26), 4.7% (2026/27)
findings.quote: The recent trend shows an average rate of growth of 10%, in line with the national trend, with a reduction in the last two years to 8% per year. For additional context, the HNB allocation from the DSG has only increased by 3% in 2024/25 and 6% in 2025/26, and 4.7% in 2026/27, highlighting the on-going budget pressures.

findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit of £18.4m by end 2025/26, forecast to rebuild to £16.7m by March 2027 despite 90% government grant funding
findings.detail: The council's cumulative DSG deficit is forecast at £18.4m by end of 2025/26, following a Q3 2025/26 overspend of £4.8m. While a government grant covering 90% of the accumulated deficit would reduce this to £1.84m at March 2026, the council forecasts a new £14.9m overspend in 2026/27, meaning the cumulative deficit rapidly rebuilds to £16.7m by March 2027. Without government support, modelling shows the deficit could reach £29m by March 2027 and £46m by end of March 2028.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand both the current scale of the deficit and its growth trajectory even with all announced mitigations in place, especially the cliff-edge risk when the statutory override ends in 2028.
findings.figures: £18.4m deficit end 2025/26; £4.8m Q3 overspend; £1.84m after 90% grant at March 2026; £14.9m forecast overspend 2026/27; £16.7m cumulative by March 2027; £29m by March 2027 and £46m by March 2028 without grant support
findings.quote: if 90% grant funding is allocated to Brent to address the cumulative deficit, the current deficit forecast of £18.4m will reduce to £1.84m at the end of March 2026. However, the current forecast overspend in 2026/27 is expected to be £14.9m based on current demand and spend projections. The cumulative deficit by March 2027 could therefore rise to £16.7m.

findings.headline: Adult social care and children's services demand growth continues with workforce and inflation pressures expected to persist.
findings.detail: Report identifies 'sustained growth in demand' for both adult and children's services, with residents living longer with complex needs. Inflation in care markets, workforce shortages and rising provider costs have 'significantly increased the price of delivering these services, and these pressures are expected to continue.' This is the core driver of the £12.5m General Fund overspend.
findings.matters: These are demand-led, open-ended commitments. If provider costs continue to outpace inflation and demand grows faster than anticipated, the council faces recurring overspends. The trend is structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: Adult social care and children's services experiencing 'sustained growth in demand'; £12.5m of 2025/26 overspend 'primarily within Adult Social Care due to increases in the cost of placements'
findings.quote: Adult social care and children's services continue to experience sustained growth in demand. More residents are living longer with complex needs, and more children and families require support. Inflation in care markets, workforce shortages and rising provider costs have significantly increased the price of delivering these services, and these pressures are expected to continue.

findings.headline: Homelessness presentations up 21% with 2,054 households in temporary accommodation and costs spiralling across London.
findings.detail: Homelessness presentations expected to reach 8,840 by end 2025/26 (21% increase). Temporary accommodation at 2,054 units, emergency accommodation up 36%. Council cites March 2025 data showing London councils spent £196m in a single month on temp accommodation (86% increase year-on-year), described as 'an unsustainable strain on public finances'.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led liability with no clear end point. Brent's trajectory mirrors the London-wide crisis. This is both an operational headwind (the £12.5m overspend is partly housing-driven) and a balance sheet risk if the council holds properties or guarantees accommodation.
findings.figures: 21% increase in homelessness presentations, 2,054 in temporary accommodation, 36% increase in emergency accommodation, March 2025 London-wide temp accommodation spend £196m (86% increase YoY)
findings.quote: The Housing Needs Service has seen a 21% increase in homelessness presentations, with cases expected to reach 8,840 by the end of 2025/26. In March 2025 alone, councils spent £196 million in a single month on temporary accommodation, an increase of 86% compared with the previous year. These costs represent both families in crisis and an unsustainable strain on public finances.

findings.headline: Savings delivery flagged as a key risk; £10.4m savings target required but explicitly acknowledged as challenging.
findings.detail: Council proposes £10.4m new savings for 2026/27. Report states: 'it must be acknowledged that delivering these savings will be challenging and non-delivery of savings is a key risk to the 2026/27 budget and the MTFS.' No detail given on what happens if savings do not land.
findings.matters: A savings plan identified upfront as high-risk signals weak confidence in delivery. If £10.4m does not materialise, council will need to either draw reserves, cut services mid-year, or seek exceptional financial support. This is a material budget headwind.
findings.figures: £10.4m savings target for 2026/27, cumulative savings £248m since 2010 (49% of net revenue budget)
findings.quote: it must be acknowledged that delivering these savings will be challenging and non-delivery of savings is a key risk to the 2026/27 budget and the MTFS.

findings.headline: £19.6m overspend forecast in current year (2025/26) with adult social care as primary driver.
findings.detail: Q3 2025/26 position shows £12.5m General Fund overspend (mainly adult social care placements and housing), £4.8m DSG overspend (£3.5m from out-of-borough school placements), and £2.3m HRA overspend. Council is managing current year but position is deteriorating.
findings.matters: An in-year overspend of this scale (on a £505m net budget) indicates underlying service cost pressures that have not been resolved and are expected to continue into 2026/27. Out-of-borough placements signal SEND capacity issues.
findings.figures: £12.5m General Fund overspend, £4.8m DSG overspend, £2.3m HRA overspend, total £19.6m in 2025/26
findings.quote: the quarter 3 position setting out the forecast overspends of £12.5m on the General Fund revenue budget, £4.8m against the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) and £2.3m on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA), for a total forecast overspend of £19.6m.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block deficit of £18.4m with contingent liability from 2028 statutory override end.
findings.detail: Cumulative deficit forecast to rise to £18.4m by end of 2025/26. Government committing to cover 90% under a statutory override, but Brent must fund the remaining 10% when the override ends March 2028. Council is setting aside £2.1m in a new reserve to meet this liability.
findings.matters: A £1.8m liability hitting in two years is a material contingent liability on the balance sheet. The government support is time-limited, creating a fixed future claim on the council's finances.
findings.figures: £18.4m cumulative deficit, 10% to be funded by council (£1.84m), government covering 90%, statutory override ends March 2028
findings.quote: The cumulative DSG High Needs Block deficit for Brent is forecast to rise to £18.4m by the end of 2025/26. It is therefore proposed to allocate the £2.1m additional RSG to create a new reserve which will hold sufficient funds to resolve the remaining 10% of the accrued deficit when the statutory override ends in March 2028.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: 9a) Budget Scrutiny Task Group Report 2026/27 , item 9.
findings.headline: 1% service efficiency requirement across all departments without detailed mitigation plans
findings.detail: The council requires every department to deliver 1% efficiency savings. Officers acknowledge this will be challenging and workforce reductions cannot be ruled out. The Task Group noted high-pressure services like Social Care face disproportionate impact.
findings.matters: Across-the-board efficiency cuts often translate to service reductions or deterioration in quality, particularly in understaffed areas. This risks regulatory findings or safeguarding failures.
findings.figures: 1% efficiency requirement across all departments; £3.20m council-wide saving from service efficiency
findings.quote: officers advised that achieving the 1% target would be challenging and acknowledged that workforce impacts, including reductions in posts or holding vacancies, could not be ruled out at this stage as part of efforts to streamline services.

findings.committee: Resources and Public Realm Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: 9a) Budget Scrutiny Task Group Report 2026/27 , item 9.
findings.headline: Housing benefit claim reduction of £270k uncertain with late review only weeks before new year begins
findings.detail: A £270k saving depends on caseload reduction by March 2026. Review will occur after budget approval in February but only weeks before 2026/27 starts, leaving no time to adjust plans if the saving does not materialise.
